pages.md: ## Representation as pointwise supremum of affine functions The examples above illustrate a good method for establishing convexity of a function: by expressing it as the pointwise supremum of a family of affine functions. Except for a technical condition, a converse holds: almost every convex function can be expressed as the pointwise supremum of a family of affine functions. For example,if \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is convex,with dom \( f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,then we have \[f\left( x\right) = \sup \{ g\left( x\right) \mid g\text{ affine, }g\left( z\right) \leq f\left( z\right) \text{ for all }z\} .\] In other words, \( f \) is the pointwise supremum of the set of all affine global under-estimators of it. We give the proof of this result below, and leave the case where dom \( f \neq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) as an exercise (exercise 3.28). Suppose \( f \) is convex with \( \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . The inequality \[f\left( x\right) \geq \sup \{ g\left( x\right) \mid g\text{ affine, }g\left( z\right) \leq f\left( z\right) \text{ for all }z\}\] is clear,since if \( g \) is any affine underestimator of \( f \) ,we have \( g\left( x\right) \leq f\left( x\right) \) . To establish equality,we will show that for each \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,there is an affine function \( g \) , which is a global underestimator of \( f \) ,and satisfies \( g\left( x\right) = f\left( x\right) \) . The epigraph of \( f \) is,of course,a convex set. Hence we can find a supporting hyperplane to it at \( \left( {x,f\left( x\right) }\right) \) ,i.e., \( a \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( b \in \mathbf{R} \) with \( \left( {a,b}\right) \neq 0 \) and \[{\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} a \\ b \end{array}\right\rbrack }^{T}\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} x - z \\ f\left( x\right) - t \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \leq 0\] for all \( \left( {z,t}\right) \in \) epi \( f \) . This means that \[{a}^{T}\left( {x - z}\right) + b\left( {f\left( x\right) - f\left( z\right) - s}\right) \leq 0 \tag{3.8}\] for all \( z \in \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and all \( s \geq 0 \) (since \( \left( {z,t}\right) \in \operatorname{epi}f \) means \( t = f\left( z\right) + s \) for some \( s \geq 0 \) ). For the inequality (3.8) to hold for all \( s \geq 0 \) ,we must have \( b \geq 0 \) . If \( b = 0 \) ,then the inequality (3.8) reduces to \( {a}^{T}\left( {x - z}\right) \leq 0 \) for all \( z \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,which implies \( a = 0 \) and contradicts \( \left( {a,b}\right) \neq 0 \) . We conclude that \( b > 0 \) ,i.e.,that the supporting hyperplane is not vertical. Using the fact that \( b > 0 \) we rewrite (3.8) for \( s = 0 \) as \[g\left( z\right) = f\left( x\right) + {\left( a/b\right) }^{T}\left( {x - z}\right) \leq f\left( z\right)\] for all \( z \) . The function \( g \) is an affine underestimator of \( f \) ,and satisfies \( g\left( x\right) = f\left( x\right) \) . #### 3.2.4 Composition In this section we examine conditions on \( h : {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) and \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) that guarantee convexity or concavity of their composition \( f = h \circ g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,defined by \[f\left( x\right) = h\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) ,\;\operatorname{dom}f = \{ x \in \operatorname{dom}g \mid g\left( x\right) \in \operatorname{dom}h\} .\]

blocks.text: Representation as pointwise supremum of affine functions

The examples above illustrate a good method for establishing convexity of a function: by expressing it as the pointwise supremum of a family of affine functions. Except for a technical condition, a converse holds: almost every convex function can be expressed as the pointwise supremum of a family of affine functions. For example,if \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is convex,with dom \( f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,then we have
\[f\left( x\right)  = \sup \{ g\left( x\right)  \mid  g\text{ affine, }g\left( z\right)  \leq  f\left( z\right) \text{ for all }z\} .\]

In other words, \( f \) is the pointwise supremum of the set of all affine global under-estimators of it. We give the proof of this result below, and leave the case where dom \( f \neq  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) as an exercise (exercise 3.28).
Suppose \( f \) is convex with \( \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . The inequality
\[f\left( x\right)  \geq  \sup \{ g\left( x\right)  \mid  g\text{ affine, }g\left( z\right)  \leq  f\left( z\right) \text{ for all }z\}\]

is clear,since if \( g \) is any affine underestimator of \( f \) ,we have \( g\left( x\right)  \leq  f\left( x\right) \) . To establish equality,we will show that for each \( x \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,there is an affine function \( g \) , which is a global underestimator of \( f \) ,and satisfies \( g\left( x\right)  = f\left( x\right) \) .

The epigraph of \( f \) is,of course,a convex set. Hence we can find a supporting hyperplane to it at \( \left( {x,f\left( x\right) }\right) \) ,i.e., \( a \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( b \in  \mathbf{R} \) with \( \left( {a,b}\right)  \neq  0 \) and
\[{\left\lbrack  \begin{array}{l} a \\  b \end{array}\right\rbrack  }^{T}\left\lbrack  \begin{matrix} x - z \\  f\left( x\right)  - t \end{matrix}\right\rbrack   \leq  0\]
for all \( \left( {z,t}\right)  \in \) epi \( f \) . This means that
\[{a}^{T}\left( {x - z}\right)  + b\left( {f\left( x\right)  - f\left( z\right)  - s}\right)  \leq  0 \]

for all \( z \in  \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and all \( s \geq  0 \) (since \( \left( {z,t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{epi}f \) means \( t = f\left( z\right)  + s \) for some \( s \geq  0 \) ). For the inequality (3.8) to hold for all \( s \geq  0 \) ,we must have \( b \geq  0 \) . If \( b = 0 \) ,then the inequality (3.8) reduces to \( {a}^{T}\left( {x - z}\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( z \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,which implies \( a = 0 \) and contradicts \( \left( {a,b}\right)  \neq  0 \) . We conclude that \( b > 0 \) ,i.e.,that the supporting hyperplane is not vertical.
Using the fact that \( b > 0 \) we rewrite (3.8) for \( s = 0 \) as
\[g\left( z\right)  = f\left( x\right)  + {\left( a/b\right) }^{T}\left( {x - z}\right)  \leq  f\left( z\right)\]
for all \( z \) . The function \( g \) is an affine underestimator of \( f \) ,and satisfies \( g\left( x\right)  = f\left( x\right) \) .

In this section we examine conditions on \( h : {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) and \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) that guarantee convexity or concavity of their composition \( f = h \circ  g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) ,defined by
\[f\left( x\right)  = h\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) ,\;\operatorname{dom}f = \{ x \in  \operatorname{dom}g \mid  g\left( x\right)  \in  \operatorname{dom}h\} .\]

pages.md: ## Scalar composition We first consider the case \( k = 1 \) ,so \( h : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) and \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) . We can restrict ourselves to the case \( n = 1 \) (since convexity is determined by the behavior of a function on arbitrary lines that intersect its domain). To discover the composition rules,we start by assuming that \( h \) and \( g \) are twice differentiable,with \( \operatorname{dom}g = \operatorname{dom}h = \mathbf{R} \) . In this case,convexity of \( f \) reduces to \( {f}^{\prime \prime } \geq 0 \) (meaning, \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) \geq 0 \) for all \( x \in \mathbf{R} \) ). The second derivative of the composition function \( f = h \circ g \) is given by \[{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) = {h}^{\prime \prime }\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) {g}^{\prime }{\left( x\right) }^{2} + {h}^{\prime }\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) {g}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) . \tag{3.9}\] Now suppose,for example,that \( g \) is convex (so \( {g}^{\prime \prime } \geq 0 \) ) and \( h \) is convex and nondecreasing (so \( {h}^{\prime \prime } \geq 0 \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \geq 0 \) ). It follows from (3.9) that \( {f}^{\prime \prime } \geq 0 \) ,i.e., \( f \) is convex. In a similar way, the expression (3.9) gives the results: \( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex and nondecreasing,and \( g \) is convex,(3.10)\( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex and nonincreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave and nondecreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave and nonincreasing,and \( g \) is convex. These statements are valid when the functions \( g \) and \( h \) are twice differentiable and have domains that are all of \( \mathbf{R} \) . It turns out that very similar composition rules hold in the general case \( n > 1 \) ,without assuming differentiability of \( h \) and \( g \) ,or that \( \operatorname{dom}g = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( \operatorname{dom}h = \mathbf{R} \) : \( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing,and \( g \) is convex,(3.11)\( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nonincreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nonincreasing,and \( g \) is convex. Here \( \widetilde{h} \) denotes the extended-value extension of the function \( h \) ,which assigns the value \( \infty \left( {-\infty }\right) \) to points not in \( \operatorname{dom}h \) for \( h \) convex (concave). The only difference between these results, and the results in (3.10), is that we require that the extended-value extension function \( \widetilde{h} \) be nonincreasing or nondecreasing,on all of \( \mathbf{R} \) . To understand what this means,suppose \( h \) is convex,so \( \widetilde{h} \) takes on the value \( \infty \) outside dom \( h \) . To say that \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing means that for any \( x,y \in \mathbf{R} \) ,with \( x < y \) ,we have \( \widetilde{h}\left( x\right) \leq \widetilde{h}\left( y\right) \) . In particular,this means that if \( y \in \operatorname{dom}h \) ,then \( x \in \) dom \( h \) . In other words,the domain of \( h \) extends infinitely in the negative direction; it is either \( \mathbf{R} \) ,or an interval of the form \( \left( {-\infty ,a}\right) \) or \( ( - \infty ,a\rbrack \) . In a similar way,to say that \( h \) is convex and \( \widetilde{h} \) is nonincreasing means that \( h \) is nonincreasing and dom \( h \) extends infinitely in the positive direction. This is illustrated in figure 3.7. --- Example 3.12 Some simple examples will illustrate the conditions on \( h \) that appear in the composition theorems. - The function \( h\left( x\right) = \log x \) ,with \( \operatorname{dom}h = {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + } \) ,is concave and satisfies \( \widetilde{h} \) nondecreasing. ---

\( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing,and \( g \) is convex, (3.11) \( f \) is convex if \( h \) is convex, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nonincreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing,and \( g \) is concave, \( f \) is concave if \( h \) is concave, \( \widetilde{h} \) is nonincreasing,and \( g \) is convex.

The composition results (3.11) can be proved directly, without assuming differentiability, or using the formula (3.9). As an example, we will prove the following composition theorem: if \( g \) is convex, \( h \) is convex,and \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing, then \( f = h \circ g \) is convex. Assume that \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq 1 \) . Since \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,we have that \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}g \) and \( g\left( x\right) ,g\left( y\right) \in \operatorname{dom}h \) . Since \( \operatorname{dom}g \) is convex,we conclude that \( {\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y \in \operatorname{dom}g \) ,and from convexity of \( g \) ,we have \[g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \leq {\theta g}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) . \tag{3.12}\] Since \( g\left( x\right) ,g\left( y\right) \in \operatorname{dom}h \) ,we conclude that \( {\theta g}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) \in \operatorname{dom}h \) ,i.e., the righthand side of (3.12) is in \( \operatorname{dom}h \) . Now we use the assumption that \( h \) is nondecreasing, which means that its domain extends infinitely in the negative direction. Since the righthand side of (3.12) is in \( \operatorname{dom}h \) ,we conclude that the lefthand side,i.e., \( g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \in \operatorname{dom}h \) . This means that \( {\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) . At this point,we have shown that \( \operatorname{dom}f \) is convex. Now using the fact that \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing and the inequality (3.12),we get \[h\left( {g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) }\right) \leq h\left( {{\theta g}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) }\right) . \tag{3.13}\] From convexity of \( h \) ,we have \[h\left( {{\theta g}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) }\right) \leq {\theta h}\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) h\left( {g\left( y\right) }\right) . \tag{3.14}\]

For example,we have \( \widetilde{h}\left( {-1}\right)  = \infty \) ,but \( \widetilde{h}\left( 1\right)  = 1 \) .

The composition results (3.11) can be proved directly, without assuming differentiability, or using the formula (3.9). As an example, we will prove the following composition theorem: if \( g \) is convex, \( h \) is convex,and \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing, then \( f = h \circ  g \) is convex. Assume that \( x,y \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) ,and \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  1 \) . Since \( x,y \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) ,we have that \( x,y \in  \operatorname{dom}g \) and \( g\left( x\right) ,g\left( y\right)  \in  \operatorname{dom}h \) . Since \( \operatorname{dom}g \) is convex,we conclude that \( {\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y \in  \operatorname{dom}g \) ,and from convexity of \( g \) ,we have
\[g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right)  \leq  {\theta g}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) . \]

Since \( g\left( x\right) ,g\left( y\right)  \in  \operatorname{dom}h \) ,we conclude that \( {\theta g}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right)  \in  \operatorname{dom}h \) ,i.e., the righthand side of (3.12) is in \( \operatorname{dom}h \) . Now we use the assumption that \( h \) is nondecreasing, which means that its domain extends infinitely in the negative direction. Since the righthand side of (3.12) is in \( \operatorname{dom}h \) ,we conclude that the lefthand side,i.e., \( g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right)  \in  \operatorname{dom}h \) . This means that \( {\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) . At this point,we have shown that \( \operatorname{dom}f \) is convex.
Now using the fact that \( \widetilde{h} \) is nondecreasing and the inequality (3.12),we get
\[h\left( {g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) }\right)  \leq  h\left( {{\theta g}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) }\right) . \]

\[h\left( {{\theta g}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( y\right) }\right)  \leq  {\theta h}\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) h\left( {g\left( y\right) }\right) . \]

pages.md: Putting (3.13) and (3.14) together, we have \[h\left( {g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) }\right) \leq {\theta h}\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) h\left( {g\left( y\right) }\right) .\] which proves the composition theorem. Example 3.13 Simple composition results. --- - If \( g \) is convex then \( \exp g\left( x\right) \) is convex. - If \( g \) is concave and positive,then \( \log g\left( x\right) \) is concave. - If \( g \) is concave and positive,then \( 1/g\left( x\right) \) is convex. - If \( g \) is convex and nonnegative and \( p \geq 1 \) ,then \( g{\left( x\right) }^{p} \) is convex. - If \( g \) is convex then \( - \log \left( {-g\left( x\right) }\right) \) is convex on \( \{ x \mid g\left( x\right) < 0\} \) . --- Remark 3.3 The requirement that monotonicity hold for the extended-value extension \( \widetilde{h} \) ,and not just the function \( h \) ,cannot be removed. For example,consider the function \( g\left( x\right) = {x}^{2} \) ,with \( \operatorname{dom}g = \mathbf{R} \) ,and \( h\left( x\right) = 0 \) ,with \( \operatorname{dom}h = \left\lbrack {1,2}\right\rbrack \) . Here \( g \) is convex, and \( h \) is convex and nondecreasing. But the function \( f = h \circ g \) ,given by \[f\left( x\right) = 0,\;\operatorname{dom}f = \left\lbrack {-\sqrt{2}, - 1}\right\rbrack \cup \left\lbrack {1,\sqrt{2}}\right\rbrack ,\] is not convex,since its domain is not convex. Here,of course,the function \( \widetilde{h} \) is not nondecreasing. ## Vector composition We now turn to the more complicated case when \( k \geq 1 \) . Suppose \[f\left( x\right) = h\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) = h\left( {{g}_{1}\left( x\right) ,\ldots ,{g}_{k}\left( x\right) }\right) ,\] with \( h : {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow \mathbf{R},{g}_{i} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) . Again without loss of generality we can assume \( n = \) 1. As in the case \( k = 1 \) ,we start by assuming the functions are twice differentiable, with \( \operatorname{dom}g = \mathbf{R} \) and \( \operatorname{dom}h = {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) ,in order to discover the composition rules. We have \[{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) = {g}^{\prime }{\left( x\right) }^{T}{\nabla }^{2}h\left( {g\left( x\right) }\right) {g}^{\prime }\left( x\right) + \nabla h{\left( g\left( x\right) \right) }^{T}{g}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) , \tag{3.15}\] which is the vector analog of (3.9). pages.md: Example 3.17 Suppose \( h \) is convex. Then the function \( g \) defined as \[g\left( x\right) = \inf \{ h\left( y\right) \mid {Ay} = x\}\] is convex. To see this,we define \( f \) by \[f\left( {x,y}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} h\left( y\right) & \text{ if }{Ay} = x \\ \infty & \text{ otherwise, } \end{array}\right.\] which is convex in \( \left( {x,y}\right) \) . Then \( g \) is the minimum of \( f \) over \( y \) ,and hence is convex. (It is not hard to show directly that \( g \) is convex.) #### 3.2.6 Perspective of a function If \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,then the perspective of \( f \) is the function \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) defined by \[g\left( {x,t}\right) = {tf}\left( {x/t}\right) ,\] with domain \[\operatorname{dom}g = \{ \left( {x,t}\right) \mid x/t \in \operatorname{dom}f,t > 0\} .\] The perspective operation preserves convexity: If \( f \) is a convex function,then so is its perspective function \( g \) . Similarly,if \( f \) is concave,then so is \( g \) . This can be proved several ways, for example, direct verification of the defining inequality (see exercise 3.33). We give a short proof here using epigraphs and the perspective mapping on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) described in \( §{2.3.3} \) (which will also explain the name ’perspective’). For \( t > 0 \) we have \[\left( {x,t,s}\right) \in \operatorname{epi}g \Leftrightarrow {tf}\left( {x/t}\right) \leq s\] \[\Leftrightarrow f\left( {x/t}\right) \leq s/t\] \[\Leftrightarrow \;\left( {x/t,s/t}\right) \in \operatorname{epi}f.\] Therefore epi \( g \) is the inverse image of epi \( f \) under the perspective mapping that takes \( \left( {u,v,w}\right) \) to \( \left( {u,w}\right) /v \) . It follows (see §2.3.3) that epi \( g \) is convex,so the function \( g \) is convex. Example 3.18 Euclidean norm squared. The perspective of the convex function \( f\left( x\right) = {x}^{T}x \) on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is \[g\left( {x,t}\right) = t{\left( x/t\right) }^{T}\left( {x/t}\right) = \frac{{x}^{T}x}{t},\] which is convex in \( \left( {x,t}\right) \) for \( t > 0 \) . We can deduce convexity of \( g \) using several other methods. First,we can express \( g \) as the sum of the quadratic-over-linear functions \( {x}_{i}^{2}/t \) ,which were shown to be convex in \( §{3.1.5} \) . We can also express \( g \) as a special case of the matrix fractional function \( {x}^{T}{\left( tI\right) }^{-1}x \) (see example 3.4).

pages.md: Example 3.19 Negative logarithm. Consider the convex function \( f\left( x\right) = - \log x \) on \( {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + } \) . Its perspective is \[g\left( {x,t}\right) = - t\log \left( {x/t}\right) = t\log \left( {t/x}\right) = t\log t - t\log x,\] and is convex on \( {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + }^{2} \) . The function \( g \) is called the relative entropy of \( t \) and \( x \) . For \( x = 1,g \) reduces to the negative entropy function. From convexity of \( g \) we can establish convexity or concavity of several interesting related functions. First,the relative entropy of two vectors \( u,v \in {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + }^{n} \) ,defined as \[\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{u}_{i}\log \left( {{u}_{i}/{v}_{i}}\right)\] is convex in \( \left( {u,v}\right) \) ,since it is a sum of relative entropies of \( {u}_{i},{v}_{i} \) . A closely related function is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between \( u,v \in {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + }^{n} \) , given by \[{D}_{\mathrm{{kl}}}\left( {u,v}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{u}_{i}\log \left( {{u}_{i}/{v}_{i}}\right) - {u}_{i} + {v}_{i}}\right) , \tag{3.17}\] which is convex,since it is the relative entropy plus a linear function of \( \left( {u,v}\right) \) . The Kullback-Leibler divergence satisfies \( {D}_{\mathrm{{kl}}}\left( {u,v}\right) \geq 0 \) ,and \( {D}_{\mathrm{{kl}}}\left( {u,v}\right) = 0 \) if and only if \( u = v \) ,and so can be used as a measure of deviation between two positive vectors; see exercise 3.13. (Note that the relative entropy and the Kullback-Leibler divergence are the same when \( u \) and \( v \) are probability vectors,i.e.,satisfy \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}u = {\mathbf{1}}^{T}v = 1 \) .) If we take \( {v}_{i} = {\mathbf{1}}^{T}u \) in the relative entropy function,we obtain the concave (and homogeneous) function of \( u \in {\mathbf{R}}_{+ + }^{n} \) given by \[\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{u}_{i}\log \left( {{\mathbf{1}}^{T}u/{u}_{i}}\right) = \left( {{\mathbf{1}}^{T}u}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{z}_{i}\log \left( {1/{z}_{i}}\right) ,\] where \( z = u/\left( {{\mathbf{1}}^{T}u}\right) \) ,which is called the normalized entropy function. The vector \( z = u/{\mathbf{1}}^{T}u \) is a normalized vector or probability distribution,since its components sum to one; the normalized entropy of \( u \) is \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}u \) times the entropy of this normalized distribution. The function \( {f}^{ * } : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,defined as \[{f}^{ * }\left( y\right) = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in \operatorname{dom}f}}\left( {{y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) }\right) , \tag{3.18}\] is called the conjugate of the function \( f \) . The domain of the conjugate function consists of \( y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) for which the supremum is finite,i.e.,for which the difference \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) is bounded above on \( \operatorname{dom}f \) . This definition is illustrated in figure 3.8. We see immediately that \( {f}^{ * } \) is a convex function,since it is the pointwise supremum of a family of convex (indeed,affine) functions of \( y \) . This is true whether or not \( f \) is convex. We start with some simple examples, and then describe some rules for conjugating functions. This allows us to derive an analytical expression for the conjugate of many common convex functions. To derive the conjugate of the log-sum-exp function \( f\left( x\right) = \log \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{e}^{{x}_{i}}}\right) \) ,we first determine the values of \( y \) for which the maximum over \( x \) of \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) is attained. By setting the gradient with respect to \( x \) equal to zero,we obtain the condition \[{y}_{i} = \frac{{e}^{{x}_{i}}}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{e}^{{x}_{j}}},\;i = 1,\ldots ,n.\] These equations are solvable for \( x \) if and only if \( y \succ 0 \) and \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y = 1 \) . By substituting the expression for \( {y}_{i} \) into \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) we obtain \( {f}^{ * }\left( y\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{y}_{i}\log {y}_{i} \) . This expression for \( {f}^{ * } \) is still correct if some components of \( y \) are zero,as long as \( y \succcurlyeq 0 \) and \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y = 1 \) , and we interpret \( 0\log 0 \) as 0 . In fact the domain of \( {f}^{ * } \) is exactly given by \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y = 1,y \succcurlyeq 0 \) . To show this,suppose that a component of \( y \) is negative,say, \( {y}_{k} < 0 \) . Then we can show that \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) is unbounded above by choosing \( {x}_{k} = - t \) ,and \( {x}_{i} = 0,i \neq k \) ,and letting \( t \) go to infinity. If \( y \succcurlyeq 0 \) but \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y \neq 1 \) ,we choose \( x = t\mathbf{1} \) ,so that \[{y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) = t{\mathbf{1}}^{T}y - t - \log n.\] If \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y > 1 \) ,this grows unboundedly as \( t \rightarrow \infty \) ; if \( {\mathbf{1}}^{T}y < 1 \) ,it grows unboundedly as \( t \rightarrow - \infty \) . In summary, \[{f}^{ * }\left( y\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{y}_{i}\log {y}_{i} & \text{ if }y \succcurlyeq 0\text{ and }{\mathbf{1}}^{T}y = 1 \\ \infty & \text{ otherwise. } \end{array}\right.\] In other words, the conjugate of the log-sum-exp function is the negative entropy function, restricted to the probability simplex. Example 3.28 Revenue and profit functions. We consider a business or enterprise that consumes \( n \) resources and produces a product that can be sold. We let \( r = \left( {{r}_{1},\ldots ,{r}_{n}}\right) \) denote the vector of resource quantities consumed,and \( S\left( r\right) \) denote the sales revenue derived from the product produced (as a function of the resources consumed). Now let \( {p}_{i} \) denote the price (per unit) of resource \( i \) ,so the total amount paid for resources by the enterprise is \( {p}^{T}r \) . The profit derived by the firm is then \( S\left( r\right) - {p}^{T}r \) . Let us fix the prices of the resources, and ask what is the maximum profit that can be made, by wisely choosing the quantities of resources consumed. This maximum profit is given by \[M\left( p\right) = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{r}\left( {S\left( r\right) - {p}^{T}r}\right) .\] The function \( M\left( p\right) \) gives the maximum profit attainable,as a function of the resource prices. pages.md: ## Differentiable functions The conjugate of a differentiable function \( f \) is also called the Legendre transform of \( f \) . (To distinguish the general definition from the differentiable case,the term Fenchel conjugate is sometimes used instead of conjugate.) Suppose \( f \) is convex and differentiable,with \( \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Any maximizer \( {x}^{ * } \) of \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) satisfies \( y = \nabla f\left( {x}^{ * }\right) \) ,and conversely,if \( {x}^{ * } \) satisfies \( y = \nabla f\left( {x}^{ * }\right) \) ,then \( {x}^{ * } \) maximizes \( {y}^{T}x - f\left( x\right) \) . Therefore,if \( y = \nabla f\left( {x}^{ * }\right) \) ,we have \[{f}^{ * }\left( y\right) = {x}^{*T}\nabla f\left( {x}^{ * }\right) - f\left( {x}^{ * }\right) .\] This allows us to determine \( {f}^{ * }\left( y\right) \) for any \( y \) for which we can solve the gradient equation \( y = \nabla f\left( z\right) \) for \( z \) . We can express this another way. Let \( z \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) be arbitrary and define \( y = \nabla f\left( z\right) \) . Then we have \[{f}^{ * }\left( y\right) = {z}^{T}\nabla f\left( z\right) - f\left( z\right) .\] ## Scaling and composition with affine transformation For \( a > 0 \) and \( b \in \mathbf{R} \) ,the conjugate of \( g\left( x\right) = {af}\left( x\right) + b \) is \( {g}^{ * }\left( y\right) = a{f}^{ * }\left( {y/a}\right) - b \) . Suppose \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is nonsingular and \( b \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Then the conjugate of \( g\left( x\right) = \; f\left( {{Ax} + b}\right) \) is \[{g}^{ * }\left( y\right) = {f}^{ * }\left( {{A}^{-T}y}\right) - {b}^{T}{A}^{-T}y,\] with \( \operatorname{dom}{g}^{ * } = {A}^{T}\operatorname{dom}{f}^{ * } \) . ## Sums of independent functions If \( f\left( {u,v}\right) = {f}_{1}\left( u\right) + {f}_{2}\left( v\right) \) ,where \( {f}_{1} \) and \( {f}_{2} \) are convex functions with conjugates \( {f}_{1}^{ * } \) and \( {f}_{2}^{ * } \) ,respectively,then \[{f}^{ * }\left( {w,z}\right) = {f}_{1}^{ * }\left( w\right) + {f}_{2}^{ * }\left( z\right) .\] In other words, the conjugate of the sum of independent convex functions is the sum of the conjugates. ('Independent' means they are functions of different variables.) ### 3.4 Quasiconvex functions #### 3.4.1 Definition and examples A function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is called quasiconvex (or unimodal) if its domain and all its sublevel sets \[{S}_{\alpha } = \{ x \in \operatorname{dom}f \mid f\left( x\right) \leq \alpha \} ,\] for \( \alpha \in \mathbf{R} \) ,are convex. A function is quasiconcave if \( - f \) is quasiconvex,i.e.,every superlevel set \( \{ x \mid f\left( x\right) \geq \alpha \} \) is convex. A function that is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave is called quasilinear. If a function \( f \) is quasilinear,then its domain, and every level set \( \{ x \mid f\left( x\right) = \alpha \} \) is convex.

Like convexity,quasiconvexity is characterized by the behavior of a function \( f \) on lines: \( f \) is quasiconvex if and only if its restriction to any line intersecting its domain is quasiconvex. In particular, quasiconvexity of a function can be verified by restricting it to an arbitrary line, and then checking quasiconvexity of the resulting function on \( \mathbf{R} \) . ## Quasiconvex functions on \( \mathbf{R} \) We can give a simple characterization of quasiconvex functions on \( \mathbf{R} \) . We consider continuous functions, since stating the conditions in the general case is cumbersome. A continuous function \( f : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is quasiconvex if and only if at least one of the following conditions holds: - \( f \) is nondecreasing - \( f \) is nonincreasing - there is a point \( c \in \operatorname{dom}f \) such that for \( t \leq c \) (and \( t \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ), \( f \) is nonincreasing,and for \( t \geq c \) (and \( t \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ), \( f \) is nondecreasing. The point \( c \) can be chosen as any point which is a global minimizer of \( f \) . Like convexity,quasiconvexity is characterized by the behavior of a function \( f \) on lines: \( f \) is quasiconvex if and only if its restriction to any line intersecting its domain is quasiconvex. In particular, quasiconvexity of a function can be verified by restricting it to an arbitrary line, and then checking quasiconvexity of the resulting function on \( \mathbf{R} \) .

We can give a simple characterization of quasiconvex functions on \( \mathbf{R} \) . We consider continuous functions, since stating the conditions in the general case is cumbersome. A continuous function \( f : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is quasiconvex if and only if at least one of the following conditions holds:

- there is a point \( c \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) such that for \( t \leq  c \) (and \( t \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) ), \( f \) is nonincreasing,and for \( t \geq  c \) (and \( t \in  \operatorname{dom}f \) ), \( f \) is nondecreasing.
The point \( c \) can be chosen as any point which is a global minimizer of \( f \) . Figure 3.11 illustrates this.

pages.md: ## Second-order conditions Now suppose \( f \) is twice differentiable. If \( f \) is quasiconvex,then for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) , and all \( y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,we have \[{y}^{T}\nabla f\left( x\right) = 0 \Rightarrow {y}^{T}{\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) y \geq 0. \tag{3.21}\] For a quasiconvex function on \( \mathbf{R} \) ,this reduces to the simple condition \[{f}^{\prime }\left( x\right) = 0 \Rightarrow {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right) \geq 0,\] i.e., at any point with zero slope, the second derivative is nonnegative. For a quasiconvex function on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,the interpretation of the condition (3.21) is a bit more complicated. As in the case \( n = 1 \) ,we conclude that whenever \( \nabla f\left( x\right) = 0 \) , we must have \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \succcurlyeq 0 \) . When \( \nabla f\left( x\right) \neq 0 \) ,the condition (3.21) means that \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \) is positive semidefinite on the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional subspace \( \nabla f{\left( x\right) }^{ \bot } \) . This implies that \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \) can have at most one negative eigenvalue. As a (partial) converse,if \( f \) satisfies \[{y}^{T}\nabla f\left( x\right) = 0 \Rightarrow {y}^{T}{\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) y > 0 \tag{3.22}\] for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) and all \( y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n},y \neq 0 \) ,then \( f \) is quasiconvex. This condition is the same as requiring \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \) to be positive definite for any point with \( \nabla f\left( x\right) = 0 \) , and for all other points,requiring \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \) to be positive definite on the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional subspace \( \nabla f{\left( x\right) }^{ \bot } \) . ## Proof of second-order conditions for quasiconvexity By restricting the function to an arbitrary line, it suffices to consider the case in which \( f : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) . We first show that if \( f : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is quasiconvex on an interval \( \left( {a,b}\right) \) ,then it must satisfy (3.21),i.e.,if \( {f}^{\prime }\left( c\right) = 0 \) with \( c \in \left( {a,b}\right) \) ,then we must have \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( c\right) \geq 0 \) . If \( {f}^{\prime }\left( c\right) = 0 \) with \( c \in \left( {a,b}\right) ,{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( c\right) < 0 \) ,then for small positive \( \epsilon \) we have \( f\left( {c - \epsilon }\right) < f\left( c\right) \) and \( f\left( {c + \epsilon }\right) < f\left( c\right) \) . It follows that the sublevel set \( \{ x \mid f\left( x\right) \leq f\left( c\right) - \epsilon \} \) is disconnected for small positive \( \epsilon \) ,and therefore not convex,which contradicts our assumption that \( f \) is quasiconvex. Now we show that if the condition (3.22) holds,then \( f \) is quasiconvex. Assume that (3.22) holds,i.e.,for each \( c \in \left( {a,b}\right) \) with \( {f}^{\prime }\left( c\right) = 0 \) ,we have \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( c\right) > 0 \) . This means that whenever the function \( {f}^{\prime } \) crosses the value 0,it is strictly increasing. Therefore it can cross the value 0 at most once. If \( {f}^{\prime } \) does not cross the value 0 at all,then \( f \) is either nonincreasing or nondecreasing on \( \left( {a,b}\right) \) ,and therefore quasiconvex. Otherwise it must cross the value 0 exactly once,say at \( c \in \left( {a,b}\right) \) . Since \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( c\right) > 0 \) ,it follows that \( {f}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \leq 0 \) for \( a < t \leq c \) ,and \( {f}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \geq 0 \) for \( c \leq t < b \) . This shows that \( f \) is quasiconvex. #### 3.4.4 Operations that preserve quasiconvexity ## Nonnegative weighted maximum A nonnegative weighted maximum of quasiconvex functions, i.e., \[f = \max \left\{ {{w}_{1}{f}_{1},\ldots ,{w}_{m}{f}_{m}}\right\} ,\]

pages.md: ### 3.5 Log-concave and log-convex functions #### 3.5.1 Definition A function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is logarithmically concave or log-concave if \( f\left( x\right) > 0 \) for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) and \( \log f \) is concave. It is said to be logarithmically convex or log-convex if \( \log f \) is convex. Thus \( f \) is log-convex if and only if \( 1/f \) is log-concave. It is convenient to allow \( f \) to take on the value zero,in which case we take \( \log f\left( x\right) = - \infty \) . In this case we say \( f \) is log-concave if the extended-value function \( \log f \) is concave. We can express log-concavity directly,without logarithms: a function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \; \mathbf{R} \) ,with convex domain and \( f\left( x\right) > 0 \) for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,is log-concave if and only if for all \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq 1 \) ,we have \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \geq f{\left( x\right) }^{\theta }f{\left( y\right) }^{1 - \theta }.\] In particular, the value of a log-concave function at the average of two points is at least the geometric mean of the values at the two points. From the composition rules we know that \( {e}^{h} \) is convex if \( h \) is convex,so a log-convex function is convex. Similarly, a nonnegative concave function is log-concave. It is also clear that a log-convex function is quasiconvex and a log-concave function is quasiconcave, since the logarithm is monotone increasing. Example 3.41 Laplace transform of a nonnegative function and the moment and cumulant generating functions. Suppose \( p : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) satisfies \( p\left( x\right) \geq 0 \) for all \( x \) . The Laplace transform of \( p \) , \[P\left( z\right) = \int p\left( x\right) {e}^{-{z}^{T}x}{dx}\] is log-convex on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . (Here \( \operatorname{dom}P \) is,naturally, \( \{ z \mid P\left( z\right) < \infty \} \) .) Now suppose \( p \) is a density,i.e.,satisfies \( \int p\left( x\right) {dx} = 1 \) . The function \( M\left( z\right) = P\left( {-z}\right) \) is called the moment generating function of the density. It gets its name from the fact that the moments of the density can be found from the derivatives of the moment generating function,evaluated at \( z = 0 \) ,e.g., \[\nabla M\left( 0\right) = \mathbf{E}v,\;{\nabla }^{2}M\left( 0\right) = \mathbf{E}v{v}^{T},\] where \( v \) is a random variable with density \( p \) . The function \( \log M\left( z\right) \) ,which is convex,is called the cumulant generating function for \( p \) ,since its derivatives give the cumulants of the density. For example,the first and second derivatives of the cumulant generating function, evaluated at zero, are the mean and covariance of the associated random variable: \[\nabla \log M\left( 0\right) = \mathbf{E}v,\;{\nabla }^{2}\log M\left( 0\right) = \mathbf{E}\left( {v - \mathbf{E}v}\right) {\left( v - \mathbf{E}v\right) }^{T}.\] ## Integration of log-concave functions In some special cases log-concavity is preserved by integration. If \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is log-concave, then \[g\left( x\right) = \int f\left( {x,y}\right) {dy}\] is a log-concave function of \( x \) (on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ). (The integration here is over \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) .) A proof of this result is not simple; see the references. This result has many important consequences, some of which we describe in the rest of this section. It implies, for example, that marginal distributions of log-concave probability densities are log-concave. It also implies that log-concavity is closed under convolution,i.e.,if \( f \) and \( g \) are log-concave on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,then so is the convolution \[\left( {f * g}\right) \left( x\right) = \int f\left( {x - y}\right) g\left( y\right) {dy}.\] (To see this,note that \( g\left( y\right) \) and \( f\left( {x - y}\right) \) are log-concave in \( \left( {x,y}\right) \) ,hence the product \( f\left( {x - y}\right) g\left( y\right) \) is; then the integration result applies.)

Variation in the manufacturing process causes the parameters of the product, when manufactured, to have the value \( x + w \) ,where \( w \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is a random vector that represents manufacturing variation, and is usually assumed to have zero mean. The yield of the manufacturing process, as a function of the nominal parameter values, is given by \[Y\left( x\right) = \mathbf{{prob}}\left( {x + w \in S}\right) ,\] where \( S \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) denotes the set of acceptable parameter values for the product,i.e., the product specifications. If the density of the manufacturing error \( w \) is log-concave (for example,Gaussian) and the set \( S \) of product specifications is convex,then the yield function \( Y \) is log-concave. This implies that the \( \alpha \) -yield region,defined as the set of nominal parameters for which the yield exceeds \( \alpha \) ,is convex. For example,the \( {95}\% \) yield region \[\{ x \mid Y\left( x\right) \geq {0.95}\} = \{ x \mid \log Y\left( x\right) \geq \log {0.95}\}\] is convex,since it is a superlevel set of the concave function \( \log Y \) .

These conditions are readily extended to the case of monotonicity with respect to a generalized inequality. A differentiable function \( f \) ,with convex domain,is \( K \) -nondecreasing if and only if \[\nabla f\left( x\right) { \succcurlyeq }_{{K}^{ * }}0 \tag{3.24}\] for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) . Note the difference with the simple scalar case: the gradient must be nonnegative in the dual inequality. For the strict case, we have the following: If \[\nabla f\left( x\right) { \succ }_{{K}^{ * }}0 \tag{3.25}\] for all \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,then \( f \) is \( K \) -increasing. As in the scalar case,the converse is not true. Let us prove these first-order conditions for monotonicity. First, assume that \( f \) satisfies (3.24) for all \( x \) ,but is not \( K \) -nondecreasing,i.e.,there exist \( x,y \) with \( x{ \preccurlyeq }_{K}y \) and \( f\left( y\right) < f\left( x\right) \) . By differentiability of \( f \) there exists a \( t \in \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack \) with \[\frac{d}{dt}f\left( {x + t\left( {y - x}\right) }\right) = \nabla f{\left( x + t\left( y - x\right) \right) }^{T}\left( {y - x}\right) < 0.\] Since \( y - x \in K \) this means \[\nabla f\left( {x + t\left( {y - x}\right) }\right) \notin {K}^{ * },\] which contradicts our assumption that (3.24) is satisfied everywhere. In a similar way it can be shown that (3.25) implies \( f \) is \( K \) -increasing. It is also straightforward to see that it is necessary that (3.24) hold everywhere. Assume (3.24) does not hold for \( x = z \) . By the definition of dual cone this means there exists a \( v \in K \) with \[\nabla f{\left( z\right) }^{T}v < 0\] Now consider \( h\left( t\right) = f\left( {z + {tv}}\right) \) as a function of \( t \) . We have \( {h}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) = \nabla f{\left( z\right) }^{T}v < 0 \) , and therefore there exists \( t > 0 \) with \( h\left( t\right) = f\left( {z + {tv}}\right) < h\left( 0\right) = f\left( z\right) \) ,which means \( f \) is not \( K \) -nondecreasing. #### 3.6.2 Convexity with respect to a generalized inequality Suppose \( K \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is a proper cone with associated generalized inequality \( { \preccurlyeq }_{K} \) . We say \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is \( K \) -convex if for all \( x,y \) ,and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq 1 \) , \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) { \preccurlyeq }_{K}{\theta f}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right) .\]

3.6.2 Convexity with respect to a generalized inequality

Suppose \( K \subseteq  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is a proper cone with associated generalized inequality \( { \preccurlyeq  }_{K} \) . We say \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is \( K \) -convex if for all \( x,y \) ,and \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  1 \) ,
\[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) { \preccurlyeq  }_{K}{\theta f}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right) .\]

pages.md: The function is strictly \( K \) -convex if \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) { \prec }_{K}{\theta f}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\] for all \( x \neq y \) and \( 0 < \theta < 1 \) . These definitions reduce to ordinary convexity and strict convexity when \( m = 1 \) (and \( K = {\mathbf{R}}_{ + } \) ). Example 3.47 Convexity with respect to componentwise inequality. A function \( f \) : \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is convex with respect to componentwise inequality (i.e.,the generalized inequality induced by \( {\mathbf{R}}_{ + }^{m} \) ) if and only if for all \( x,y \) and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq 1 \) , \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \preccurlyeq {\theta f}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right) ,\] i.e.,each component \( {f}_{i} \) is a convex function. The function \( f \) is strictly convex with respect to componentwise inequality if and only if each component \( {f}_{i} \) is strictly convex. Example 3.48 Matrix convexity. Suppose \( f \) is a symmetric matrix valued function, i.e., \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{S}}^{m} \) . The function \( f \) is convex with respect to matrix inequality if \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \preccurlyeq {\theta f}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\] for any \( x \) and \( y \) ,and for \( \theta \in \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . This is sometimes called matrix convexity. An equivalent definition is that the scalar function \( {z}^{T}f\left( x\right) z \) is convex for all vectors \( z \) . (This is often a good way to prove matrix convexity). A matrix function is strictly matrix convex if \[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) \prec {\theta f}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\] when \( x \neq y \) and \( 0 < \theta < 1 \) ,or,equivalently,if \( {z}^{T}{fz} \) is strictly convex for every \( z \neq 0 \) . Some examples: - The function \( f\left( X\right) = X{X}^{T} \) where \( X \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times m} \) is matrix convex,since for fixed \( z \) the function \( {z}^{T}X{X}^{T}z = {\begin{Vmatrix}{X}^{T}z\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2} \) is a convex quadratic function of (the components of) \( X \) . For the same reason, \( f\left( X\right) = {X}^{2} \) is matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . - The function \( {X}^{p} \) is matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) for \( 1 \leq p \leq 2 \) or \( - 1 \leq p \leq 0 \) ,and matrix concave for \( 0 \leq p \leq 1 \) . - The function \( f\left( X\right) = {e}^{X} \) is not matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,for \( n \geq 2 \) . Many of the results for convex functions have extensions to \( K \) -convex functions. As a simple example,a function is \( K \) -convex if and only if its restriction to any line in its domain is \( K \) -convex. In the rest of this section we list a few results for \( K \) -convexity that we will use later; more results are explored in the exercises. ## Dual characterization of \( K \) -convexity A function \( f \) is \( K \) -convex if and only if for every \( w{ \succcurlyeq }_{{K}^{ * }}0 \) ,the (real-valued) function \( {w}^{T}f \) is convex (in the ordinary sense); \( f \) is strictly \( K \) -convex if and only if for every nonzero \( w{ \succcurlyeq }_{{K}^{ * }}0 \) the function \( {w}^{T}f \) is strictly convex. (These follow directly from the definitions and properties of dual inequality.)

\[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right) { \prec  }_{K}{\theta f}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\]
for all \( x \neq  y \) and \( 0 < \theta  < 1 \) . These definitions reduce to ordinary convexity and strict convexity when \( m = 1 \) (and \( K = {\mathbf{R}}_{ + } \) ).

Example 3.47 Convexity with respect to componentwise inequality. A function \( f \) : \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is convex with respect to componentwise inequality (i.e.,the generalized inequality induced by \( {\mathbf{R}}_{ + }^{m} \) ) if and only if for all \( x,y \) and \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  1 \) ,
\[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right)  \preccurlyeq  {\theta f}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right) ,\]

i.e.,each component \( {f}_{i} \) is a convex function. The function \( f \) is strictly convex with respect to componentwise inequality if and only if each component \( {f}_{i} \) is strictly convex.

Example 3.48 Matrix convexity. Suppose \( f \) is a symmetric matrix valued function, i.e., \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{S}}^{m} \) . The function \( f \) is convex with respect to matrix inequality if
\[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right)  \preccurlyeq  {\theta f}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\]

for any \( x \) and \( y \) ,and for \( \theta  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . This is sometimes called matrix convexity. An equivalent definition is that the scalar function \( {z}^{T}f\left( x\right) z \) is convex for all vectors \( z \) . (This is often a good way to prove matrix convexity). A matrix function is strictly matrix convex if
\[f\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y}\right)  \prec  {\theta f}\left( x\right)  + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) f\left( y\right)\]
when \( x \neq  y \) and \( 0 < \theta  < 1 \) ,or,equivalently,if \( {z}^{T}{fz} \) is strictly convex for every \( z \neq  0 \) . Some examples:

- The function \( f\left( X\right)  = X{X}^{T} \) where \( X \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times  m} \) is matrix convex,since for fixed \( z \) the function \( {z}^{T}X{X}^{T}z = {\begin{Vmatrix}{X}^{T}z\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2} \) is a convex quadratic function of (the components of) \( X \) . For the same reason, \( f\left( X\right)  = {X}^{2} \) is matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) .
- The function \( {X}^{p} \) is matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) for \( 1 \leq  p \leq  2 \) or \( - 1 \leq  p \leq  0 \) ,and matrix concave for \( 0 \leq  p \leq  1 \) .
- The function \( f\left( X\right)  = {e}^{X} \) is not matrix convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,for \( n \geq  2 \) .

Many of the results for convex functions have extensions to \( K \) -convex functions. As a simple example,a function is \( K \) -convex if and only if its restriction to any line in its domain is \( K \) -convex. pages.md: ## Differentiable \( K \) -convex functions A differentiable function \( f \) is \( K \) -convex if and only if its domain is convex,and for all \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) , \[f\left( y\right) { \succcurlyeq }_{K}f\left( x\right) + {Df}\left( x\right) \left( {y - x}\right) .\] (Here \( {Df}\left( x\right) \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) is the derivative or Jacobian matrix of \( f \) at \( x \) ; see §A.4.1.) The function \( f \) is strictly \( K \) -convex if and only if for all \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) with \( x \neq y \) , \[f\left( y\right) { \succ }_{K}f\left( x\right) + {Df}\left( x\right) \left( {y - x}\right) .\] ## Composition theorem Many of the results on composition can be generalized to \( K \) -convexity. For example, if \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{p} \) is \( K \) -convex, \( h : {\mathbf{R}}^{p} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is convex,and \( \widetilde{h} \) (the extended-value extension of \( h \) ) is \( K \) -nondecreasing,then \( h \circ g \) is convex. This generalizes the fact that a nondecreasing convex function of a convex function is convex. The condition that \( \widetilde{h} \) be \( K \) -nondecreasing implies that \( \operatorname{dom}h - K = \operatorname{dom}h \) . Example 3.49 The quadratic matrix function \( g : {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) defined by --- \[g\left( X\right) = {X}^{T}{AX} + {B}^{T}X + {X}^{T}B + C,\] where \( A \in {\mathbf{S}}^{m},B \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) ,and \( C \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,is convex when \( A \succcurlyeq 0 \) . The function \( h : {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) defined by \( h\left( Y\right) = - \log \det \left( {-Y}\right) \) is convex and increasing on \( \operatorname{dom}h = - {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . By the composition theorem, we conclude that \[f\left( X\right) = - \log \det \left( {-\left( {{X}^{T}{AX} + {B}^{T}X + {X}^{T}B + C}\right) }\right)\] is convex on \[\operatorname{dom}f = \left\{ {X \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \mid {X}^{T}{AX} + {B}^{T}X + {X}^{T}B + C \prec 0}\right\} .\] This generalizes the fact that \[- \log \left( {-\left( {a{x}^{2} + {bx} + c}\right) }\right)\] is convex on \[\{ x \in \mathbf{R} \mid a{x}^{2} + {bx} + c < 0\} ,\] provided \( a \geq 0 \) . ---

pages.md: ## Bibliography The standard reference on convex analysis is Rockafellar [Roc70]. Other books on convex functions are Stoer and Witzgall [SW70], Roberts and Varberg [RV73], Van Tiel [vT84], Hiriart-Urruty and Lemaréchal [HUL93], Ekeland and Témam [ET99], Borwein and Lewis [BL00], Florenzano and Le Van [FL01], Barvinok [Bar02], and Bertsekas, Nedić, and Ozdaglar [Ber03]. Most nonlinear programming texts also include chapters on convex functions (see, for example, Mangasarian [Man94], Bazaraa, Sherali, and Shetty [BSS93], Bertsekas [Ber99], Polyak [Pol87], and Peressini, Sullivan, and Uhl [PSU88]). Jensen's inequality appears in [Jen06]. A general study of inequalities, in which Jensen's inequality plays a central role, is presented by Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya [HLP52], and Beckenbach and Bellman [BB65]. The term perspective function is from Hiriart-Urruty and Lemaréchal [HUL93, volume 1, page 100]. For the definitions in example 3.19 (relative entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence), and the related exercise 3.13, see Cover and Thomas [CT91]. Some important early references on quasiconvex functions (as well as other extensions of convexity) are Nikaidô [Nik54], Mangasarian [Man94, chapter 9], Arrow and Enthoven [AE61], Ponstein [Pon67], and Luenberger [Lue68]. For a more comprehensive reference list, we refer to Bazaraa, Sherali, and Shetty [BSS93, page 126]. Prékopa [Pré80] gives a survey of log-concave functions. Log-convexity of the Laplace transform is mentioned in Barndorff-Nielsen [BN78, §7]. For a proof of the integration result of log-concave functions, see Prékopa [Pré71, Pré73]. Generalized inequalities are used extensively in the recent literature on cone programming, starting with Nesterov and Nemirovski [NN94, page 156]; see also Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [BTN01] and the references at the end of chapter 4. Convexity with respect to generalized inequalities also appears in the work of Luenberger [Lue69, §8.2] and Isii [Isi64]. Matrix monotonicity and matrix convexity are attributed to Löwner [Löw34], and are discussed in detail by Davis [Dav63], Roberts and Varberg [RV73, page 216] and Marshall and Olkin [MO79, \( §{16}\mathrm{E} \) ]. For the result on convexity and concavity of the function \( {X}^{p} \) in example 3.48, see Bondar [Bon94, theorem 16.1]. For a simple example that demonstrates that \( {e}^{X} \) is not matrix convex,see Marshall and Olkin [MO79,page 474].

pages.md: 3.25 Maximum probability distance between distributions. Let \( p,q \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) represent two probability distributions on \( \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} \) (so \( p,q \succcurlyeq 0,{\mathbf{1}}^{T}p = {\mathbf{1}}^{T}q = 1 \) ). We define the maximum probability distance \( {d}_{\mathrm{{mp}}}\left( {p,q}\right) \) between \( p \) and \( q \) as the maximum difference in probability assigned by \( p \) and \( q \) ,over all events: \[{d}_{\mathrm{{mp}}}\left( {p,q}\right) = \max \{ \left| {\operatorname{prob}\left( {p,C}\right) - \operatorname{prob}\left( {q,C}\right) }\right| \mid C \subseteq \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} \} .\] Here \( \operatorname{prob}\left( {p,C}\right) \) is the probability of \( C \) ,under the distribution \( p \) ,i.e., \( \operatorname{prob}\left( {p,C}\right) = \; \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \in C}}{p}_{i} \) Find a simple expression for \( {d}_{\mathrm{{mp}}} \) ,involving \( \parallel p - q{\parallel }_{1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left| {{p}_{i} - {q}_{i}}\right| \) ,and show that \( {d}_{\mathrm{{mp}}} \) is a convex function on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . (Its domain is \( \{ \left( {p,q}\right) \mid p,q \succcurlyeq 0,{\mathbf{1}}^{T}p = {\mathbf{1}}^{T}q = 1\} \) ,but it has a natural extension to all of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .) 3.26 More functions of eigenvalues. Let \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( X\right) \geq {\lambda }_{2}\left( X\right) \geq \cdots \geq {\lambda }_{n}\left( X\right) \) denote the eigenvalues of a matrix \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . We have already seen several functions of the eigenvalues that are convex or concave functions of \( X \) . - The maximum eigenvalue \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( X\right) \) is convex (example 3.10). The minimum eigenvalue \( {\lambda }_{n}\left( X\right) \) is concave. - The sum of the eigenvalues (or trace), \( \operatorname{tr}X = {\lambda }_{1}\left( X\right) + \cdots + {\lambda }_{n}\left( X\right) \) ,is linear. - The sum of the inverses of the eigenvalues (or trace of the inverse), \( \operatorname{tr}\left( {X}^{-1}\right) = \; \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}1/{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \) ,is convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) (exercise 3.18). - The geometric mean of the eigenvalues, \( {\left( \det X\right) }^{1/n} = {\left( \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \right) }^{1/n} \) ,and the logarithm of the product of the eigenvalues, \( \log \det X = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \) ,are concave on \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) (exercise 3.18 and page 74). In this problem we explore some more functions of eigenvalues, by exploiting variational characterizations. (a) Sum of \( k \) largest eigenvalues. Show that \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \) is convex on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . Hint. [HJ85, page 191] Use the variational characterization \[\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) = \sup \left\{ {\operatorname{tr}\left( {{V}^{T}{XV}}\right) \mid V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times k},{V}^{T}V = I}\right\} .\] (b) Geometric mean of \( k \) smallest eigenvalues. Show that \( {\left( \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = n - k + 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \right) }^{1/k} \) is concave on \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . Hint. [MO79,page 513] For \( X \succ 0 \) ,we have \[{\left( \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = n - k + 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \right) }^{1/k} = \frac{1}{k}\inf \left\{ {\operatorname{tr}\left( {{V}^{T}{XV}}\right) \mid V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times k},\det {V}^{T}V = 1}\right\} .\] (c) Log of product of \( k \) smallest eigenvalues. Show that \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = n - k + 1}}^{n}\log {\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) \) is concave on \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . Hint. [MO79,page 513] For \( X \succ 0 \) , \[\mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = n - k + 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\left( X\right) = \inf \left\{ {\left. {\mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\left( {V}^{T}XV\right) }_{ii}}\right| \;V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times k},{V}^{T}V = I}\right\} .\] 3.27 Diagonal elements of Cholesky factor. Each \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) has a unique Cholesky factorization \( X = L{L}^{T} \) ,where \( L \) is lower triangular,with \( {L}_{ii} > 0 \) . pages.md: ## Operations that preserve convexity 3.28 Expressing a convex function as the pointwise supremum of a family of affine functions. In this problem we extend the result proved on page 83 to the case where \( \operatorname{dom}f \neq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Let \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) be a convex function. Define \( \widetilde{f} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) as the pointwise supremum of all affine functions that are global underestimators of \( f \) : \[\widetilde{f}\left( x\right) = \sup \{ g\left( x\right) \mid g\text{ affine, }g\left( z\right) \leq f\left( z\right) \text{ for all }z\} .\] (a) Show that \( f\left( x\right) = \widetilde{f}\left( x\right) \) for \( x \in \mathbf{{intdom}}f \) . (b) Show that \( f = \widetilde{f} \) if \( f \) is closed (i.e., \( \mathbf{{epi}}f \) is a closed set; see §A.3.3). 3.29 Representation of piecewise-linear convex functions. A convex function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,with dom \( f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,is called piecewise-linear if there exists a partition of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) as \[{\mathbf{R}}^{n} = {X}_{1} \cup {X}_{2} \cup \cdots \cup {X}_{L}\] where int \( {X}_{i} \neq \varnothing \) and int \( {X}_{i} \cap \) int \( {X}_{j} = \varnothing \) for \( i \neq j \) ,and a family of affine functions \( {a}_{1}^{T}x + {b}_{1},\ldots ,{a}_{L}^{T}x + {b}_{L} \) such that \( f\left( x\right) = {a}_{i}^{T}x + {b}_{i} \) for \( x \in {X}_{i} \) . Show that such a function has the form \( f\left( x\right) = \max \left\{ {{a}_{1}^{T}x + {b}_{1},\ldots ,{a}_{L}^{T}x + {b}_{L}}\right\} \) . 3.30 Convex hull or envelope of a function. The convex hull or convex envelope of a function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is defined as \[g\left( x\right) = \inf \{ t \mid \left( {x,t}\right) \in \mathbf{{convepi}}f\} .\] Geometrically,the epigraph of \( g \) is the convex hull of the epigraph of \( f \) . Show that \( g \) is the largest convex underestimator of \( f \) . In other words,show that if \( h \) is convex and satisfies \( h\left( x\right) \leq f\left( x\right) \) for all \( x \) ,then \( h\left( x\right) \leq g\left( x\right) \) for all \( x \) . 3.31 [Roc70,page 35] Largest homogeneous underestimator. Let \( f \) be a convex function. Define the function \( g \) as \[g\left( x\right) = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\alpha > 0}}\frac{f\left( {\alpha x}\right) }{\alpha }.\] (a) Show that \( g \) is homogeneous \( \left( {g\left( {tx}\right) = {tg}\left( x\right) \text{ for all }t \geq 0}\right) \) . (b) Show that \( g \) is the largest homogeneous underestimator of \( f \) : If \( h \) is homogeneous and \( h\left( x\right) \leq f\left( x\right) \) for all \( x \) ,then we have \( h\left( x\right) \leq g\left( x\right) \) for all \( x \) . (c) Show that \( g \) is convex. 3.32 Products and ratios of convex functions. In general the product or ratio of two convex functions is not convex. However, there are some results that apply to functions on R. Prove the following. (a) If \( f \) and \( g \) are convex,both nondecreasing (or nonincreasing),and positive functions on an interval,then \( {fg} \) is convex. (b) If \( f,g \) are concave,positive,with one nondecreasing and the other nonincreasing, then \( {fg} \) is concave. (c) If \( f \) is convex,nondecreasing,and positive,and \( g \) is concave,nonincreasing,and positive,then \( f/g \) is convex. 3.33 Direct proof of perspective theorem. Give a direct proof that the perspective function \( g \) , as defined in \( §{3.2.6} \) ,of a convex function \( f \) is convex: Show that \( \operatorname{dom}g \) is a convex set, and that for \( \left( {x,t}\right) ,\left( {y,s}\right) \in \operatorname{dom}g \) ,and \( 0 \leq \theta \leq 1 \) ,we have \[g\left( {{\theta x} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) y,{\theta t} + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) s}\right) \leq {\theta g}\left( {x,t}\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) g\left( {y,s}\right) .\] 3.34 The Minkowski function. The Minkowski function of a convex set \( C \) is defined as \[{M}_{C}\left( x\right) = \inf \left\{ {t > 0 \mid {t}^{-1}x \in C}\right\} .\]

(a) Max function. \( f\left( x\right) = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots ,n}}{x}_{i} \) on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Let \( {f}_{0},\ldots ,{f}_{n} : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) be given continuous functions. We consider the problem of approximating \( {f}_{0} \) as a linear combination of \( {f}_{1},\ldots ,{f}_{n} \) . For \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,we say that \( f = {x}_{1}{f}_{1} + \cdots + {x}_{n}{f}_{n} \) approximates \( {f}_{0} \) with tolerance \( \epsilon > 0 \) over the interval \( \left\lbrack {0,T}\right\rbrack \) if \( \left| {f\left( t\right) - {f}_{0}\left( t\right) }\right| \leq \epsilon \) for \( 0 \leq t \leq T \) . Now we choose a fixed tolerance \( \epsilon > 0 \) and define the approximation width as the largest \( T \) such that \( f \) approximates \( {f}_{0} \) over the interval \( \left\lbrack {0,T}\right\rbrack \) : \[W\left( x\right) = \sup \left\{ {T\left| \right| {x}_{1}{f}_{1}\left( t\right) + \cdots + {x}_{n}{f}_{n}\left( t\right) - {f}_{0}\left( t\right) \mid \leq \epsilon \text{ for }0 \leq t \leq T}\right\} .\] Show that \( W \) is quasiconcave. 3.43 First-order condition for quasiconvexity. Prove the first-order condition for quasiconvexity given in \( §{3.4.3} \) : A differentiable function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,with \( \operatorname{dom}f \) convex,is quasiconvex if and only if for all \( x,y \in \operatorname{dom}f \) , \[f\left( y\right) \leq f\left( x\right) \Rightarrow \nabla f{\left( x\right) }^{T}\left( {y - x}\right) \leq 0.\] Hint. It suffices to prove the result for a function on \( \mathbf{R} \) ; the general result follows by restriction to an arbitrary line. 3.44 Second-order conditions for quasiconvexity. In this problem we derive alternate representations of the second-order conditions for quasiconvexity given in §3.4.3. Prove the following. We can assume without loss of generality that \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \) is diagonal.

In other words,a quasilinear function with domain \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) must be a monotone function of a linear function. ## Chapter 4 Convex optimization problems

### 4.1 Optimization problems

#### 4.1.1 Basic terminology

We use the notation

\[\text{ minimize }{f}_{0}\left( x\right)\]

\[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( x\right)  \leq  0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m \tag{4.1}\]

\[{h}_{i}\left( x\right)  = 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,p\]

to describe the problem of finding an \( x \) that minimizes \( {f}_{0}\left( x\right) \) among all \( x \) that satisfy the conditions \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right)  \leq  0,i = 1,\ldots ,m \) ,and \( {h}_{i}\left( x\right)  = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p \) . We call \( x \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) the optimization variable and the function \( {f}_{0} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) the objective function or cost function. The inequalities \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right)  \leq  0 \) are called inequality constraints,and the corresponding functions \( {f}_{i} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) are called the inequality constraint functions. The equations \( {h}_{i}\left( x\right)  = 0 \) are called the equality constraints,and the functions \( {h}_{i} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) are the equality constraint functions. If there are no constraints (i.e., \( m = p = 0 \) ) we say the problem (4.1) is unconstrained.

The set of points for which the objective and all constraint functions are defined,

\[\mathcal{D} = \mathop{\bigcap }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}\operatorname{dom}{f}_{i} \cap  \mathop{\bigcap }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}\operatorname{dom}{h}_{i}\]

is called the domain of the optimization problem (4.1). A point \( x \in  \mathcal{D} \) is feasible if it satisfies the constraints \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right)  \leq  0,i = 1,\ldots ,m \) ,and \( {h}_{i}\left( x\right)  = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p \) . The problem (4.1) is said to be feasible if there exists at least one feasible point, and infeasible otherwise. The set of all feasible points is called the feasible set or the constraint set.

The optimal value \( {p}^{ \star  } \) of the problem (4.1) is defined as

\[{p}^{ \star  } = \inf \left\{  {{f}_{0}\left( x\right)  \mid  {f}_{i}\left( x\right)  \leq  0,i = 1,\ldots ,m,{h}_{i}\left( x\right)  = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p}\right\}  .\]

We allow \( {p}^{ \star  } \) to take on the extended values \( \pm  \infty \) . If the problem is infeasible,we have \( {p}^{ \star  } = \infty \) (following the standard convention that the infimum of the empty set is \( \infty ) \) . If there are feasible points \( {x}_{k} \) with \( {f}_{0}\left( {x}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow   - \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) ,then \( {p}^{ \star  } =  - \infty \) , and we say the problem (4.1) is unbounded below.

pages.md: ## Optimal and locally optimal points We say \( {x}^{ \star } \) is an optimal point,or solves the problem (4.1),if \( {x}^{ \star } \) is feasible and \( {f}_{0}\left( {x}^{ \star }\right) = {p}^{ \star } \) . The set of all optimal points is the optimal set,denoted \[{X}_{\text{ opt }} = \left\{ {x \mid {f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0,i = 1,\ldots ,m,{h}_{i}\left( x\right) = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p,{f}_{0}\left( x\right) = {p}^{ \star }}\right\} .\] If there exists an optimal point for the problem (4.1), we say the optimal value is attained or achieved,and the problem is solvable. If \( {X}_{\text{ opt }} \) is empty,we say the optimal value is not attained or not achieved. (This always occurs when the problem is unbounded below.) A feasible point \( x \) with \( {f}_{0}\left( x\right) \leq {p}^{ \star } + \epsilon \) (where \( \epsilon > 0 \) ) is called \( \epsilon \) -suboptimal,and the set of all \( \epsilon \) -suboptimal points is called the \( \epsilon \) -suboptimal set for the problem (4.1). We say a feasible point \( x \) is locally optimal if there is an \( R > 0 \) such that \[{f}_{0}\left( x\right) = \inf \left\{ {{f}_{0}\left( z\right) \mid {f}_{i}\left( z\right) \leq 0,i = 1,\ldots ,m,}\right.\] \[\left. {{h}_{i}\left( z\right) = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p,\parallel z - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq R}\right\} ,\] or,in other words, \( x \) solves the optimization problem \[\text{ minimize }{f}_{0}\left( z\right)\] \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( z\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\] \[{h}_{i}\left( z\right) = 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,p\] \[\parallel z - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq R\] with variable \( z \) . Roughly speaking,this means \( x \) minimizes \( {f}_{0} \) over nearby points in the feasible set. The term 'globally optimal' is sometimes used for 'optimal' to distinguish between 'locally optimal' and 'optimal'. Throughout this book, however, optimal will mean globally optimal. If \( x \) is feasible and \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right) = 0 \) ,we say the \( i \) th inequality constraint \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0 \) is active at \( x \) . If \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right) < 0 \) ,we say the constraint \( {f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0 \) is inactive. (The equality constraints are active at all feasible points.) We say that a constraint is redundant if deleting it does not change the feasible set. Consider a problem with strictly convex quadratic objective, with some of the variables unconstrained: \[\text{ minimize }\;{x}_{1}^{T}{P}_{11}{x}_{1} + 2{x}_{1}^{T}{P}_{12}{x}_{2} + {x}_{2}^{T}{P}_{22}{x}_{2}\] \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( {x}_{1}\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\text{ , }\] where \( {P}_{11} \) and \( {P}_{22} \) are symmetric. Here we can analytically minimize over \( {x}_{2} \) : \[\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x}_{2}}\left( {{x}_{1}^{T}{P}_{11}{x}_{1} + 2{x}_{1}^{T}{P}_{12}{x}_{2} + {x}_{2}^{T}{P}_{22}{x}_{2}}\right) = {x}_{1}^{T}\left( {{P}_{11} - {P}_{12}{P}_{22}^{-1}{P}_{12}^{T}}\right) {x}_{1}\] (see \( § \) A.5.5). Therefore the original problem is equivalent to \[\text{ minimize }\;{x}_{1}^{T}\left( {{P}_{11} - {P}_{12}{P}_{22}^{-1}{P}_{12}^{T}}\right) {x}_{1}\] \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( {x}_{1}\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\text{ . }\] ## Epigraph problem form The epigraph form of the standard problem (4.1) is the problem \[\text{ minimize }t\] (4.11) \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{0}\left( x\right) - t \leq 0\] \[{f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\] \[{h}_{i}\left( x\right) = 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,p,\] with variables \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( t \in \mathbf{R} \) . We can easily see that it is equivalent to the original problem: \( \left( {x,t}\right) \) is optimal for (4.11) if and only if \( x \) is optimal for (4.1) and \( t = {f}_{0}\left( x\right) \) . Note that the objective function of the epigraph form problem is a linear function of the variables \( x,t \) . The epigraph form problem (4.11) can be interpreted geometrically as an optimization problem in the ’graph space’ \( \left( {x,t}\right) \) : we minimize \( t \) over the epigraph of \( {f}_{0} \) ,subject to the constraints on \( x \) . This is illustrated in figure 4.1. ## Implicit and explicit constraints By a simple trick already mentioned in \( §{3.1.2} \) ,we can include any of the constraints implicitly in the objective function, by redefining its domain. As an extreme example, the standard form problem can be expressed as the unconstrained problem \[\text{ minimize }F\left( x\right) \text{ , } \tag{4.12}\] where we define the function \( F \) as \( {f}_{0} \) ,but with domain restricted to the feasible set: \[\operatorname{dom}F = \left\{ {x \in \operatorname{dom}{f}_{0} \mid {f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0,i = 1,\ldots ,m,{h}_{i}\left( x\right) = 0,i = 1,\ldots ,p}\right\} ,\] and \( F\left( x\right) = {f}_{0}\left( x\right) \) for \( x \in \operatorname{dom}F \) . (Equivalently,we can define \( F\left( x\right) \) to have value \( \infty \) for \( x \) not feasible.) The problems (4.1) and (4.12) are clearly equivalent: they have the same feasible set, optimal points, and optimal value. Of course this transformation is nothing more than a notational trick. Making the constraints implicit has not made the problem any easier to analyze or solve, even though the problem (4.12) is, at least nominally, unconstrained. In some ways the transformation makes the problem more difficult. Suppose, for example, that the objective \( {f}_{0} \) in the original problem is differentiable,so in particular its domain is open. The restricted objective function \( F \) is probably not differentiable,since its domain is likely not to be open.

pages.md: #### 4.1.4 Parameter and oracle problem descriptions For a problem in the standard form (4.1), there is still the question of how the objective and constraint functions are specified. In many cases these functions have some analytical or closed form, i.e., are given by a formula or expression that involves the variable \( x \) as well as some parameters. Suppose,for example,the objective is quadratic,so it has the form \( {f}_{0}\left( x\right) = \left( {1/2}\right) {x}^{T}{Px} + {q}^{T}x + r \) . To specify the objective function we give the coefficients (also called problem parameters or problem data) \( P \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n},q \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,and \( r \in \mathbf{R} \) . We call this a parameter problem description, since the specific problem to be solved (i.e., the problem instance) is specified by giving the values of the parameters that appear in the expressions for the objective and constraint functions. In other cases the objective and constraint functions are described by oracle models (which are also called black box or subroutine models). In an oracle model, we do not know \( f \) explicitly,but can evaluate \( f\left( x\right) \) (and usually also some derivatives) at any \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) . This is referred to as querying the oracle,and is usually associated with some cost, such as time. We are also given some prior information about the function, such as convexity and a bound on its values. As a concrete example of an oracle model, consider an unconstrained problem, in which we are to minimize the function \( f \) . The function value \( f\left( x\right) \) and its gradient \( \nabla f\left( x\right) \) are evaluated in a subroutine. We can call the subroutine at any \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,but do not have access to its source code. Calling the subroutine with argument \( x \) yields (when the subroutine returns) \( f\left( x\right) \) and \( \nabla f\left( x\right) \) . Note that in the oracle model, we never really know the function; we only know the function value (and some derivatives) at the points where we have queried the oracle. (We also know some given prior information about the function, such as differentiability and convexity.) In practice the distinction between a parameter and oracle problem description is not so sharp. If we are given a parameter problem description, we can construct an oracle for it, which simply evaluates the required functions and derivatives when queried. Most of the algorithms we study in part III work with an oracle model, but can be made more efficient when they are restricted to solve a specific parametrized family of problems. ### 4.2 Convex optimization #### 4.2.1 Convex optimization problems in standard form A convex optimization problem is one of the form \[\text{ minimize }{f}_{0}\left( x\right)\] \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m \tag{4.15}\] \[{a}_{i}^{T}x = {b}_{i},\;i = 1,\ldots ,p,\] where \( {f}_{0},\ldots ,{f}_{m} \) are convex functions. Comparing (4.15) with the general standard form problem (4.1), the convex problem has three additional requirements:
