(We already know that the duality gap,which is \( m/t \) ,decreases as \( t \) increases.) 11.8 Predictor-corrector method for centering problems. In the standard barrier method, \( {x}^{ \star }\left( {\mu t}\right) \) is computed using Newton’s method,starting from the initial point \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) . One alternative that has been proposed is to make an approximation or prediction \( \widehat{x} \) of \( {x}^{ \star }\left( {\mu t}\right) \) ,and then start the Newton method for computing \( {x}^{ \star }\left( {\mu t}\right) \) from \( \widehat{x} \) . The idea is that this should reduce the number of Newton steps,since \( \widehat{x} \) is (presumably) a better initial point than \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) . This method of centering is called a predictor-corrector method,since it first makes a prediction of what \( {x}^{ \star }\left( {\mu t}\right) \) is,then corrects the prediction using Newton’s method. The most widely used predictor is the first-order predictor, based on the tangent to the central path, explored in exercise 11.7. This predictor is given by \[\widehat{x} = {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) + \frac{d{x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }{dt}\left( {{\mu t} - t}\right) .\] Derive an expression for the first-order predictor \( \widehat{x} \) . Compare it to the Newton update obtained,i.e., \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) + \Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}} \) ,where \( \Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}} \) is the Newton step for \( {\mu t}{f}_{0}\left( x\right) + \phi \left( x\right) \) ,at \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) . What can you say when the objective \( {f}_{0} \) is linear? (For simplicity,you can consider a problem without equality constraints.) 11.9 Dual feasible points near the central path. Consider the problem \[\text{ minimize }{f}_{0}\left( x\right)\] \[\text{ subject to }{f}_{i}\left( x\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\text{ , }\] with variable \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . We assume the functions \( {f}_{i} \) are convex and twice differentiable. (We assume for simplicity there are no equality constraints.) Recall (from §11.2.2, page 565) that \( {\lambda }_{i} = - 1/\left( {t{f}_{i}\left( {{x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) }\right) ,i = 1,\ldots ,m \) ,is dual feasible,and in fact, \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) minimizes \( L\left( {x,\lambda }\right) \) . This allows us to evaluate the dual function for \( \lambda \) ,which turns out to be \( g\left( \lambda \right) = \; {f}_{0}\left( {{x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) - m/t \) . In particular,we conclude that \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) is \( m/t \) -suboptimal. In this problem we consider what happens when a point \( x \) is close to \( {x}^{ \star }\left( t\right) \) ,but not quite centered. (This would occur if the centering steps were terminated early, or not carried out to full accuracy.) In this case,of course,we cannot claim that \( {\lambda }_{i} = - 1/\left( {t{f}_{i}\left( x\right) }\right) \) , \( i = 1,\ldots ,m \) ,is dual feasible,or that \( x \) is \( m/t \) -suboptimal. However,it turns out that a slightly more complicated formula does yield a dual feasible point,provided \( x \) is close enough to centered. Let \( \Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}} \) be the Newton step at \( x \) of the centering problem \[\text{ minimize }\;t{f}_{0}\left( x\right) - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\log \left( {-{f}_{i}\left( x\right) }\right) \text{ . }\] A formula that often gives a dual feasible point when \( \Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}} \) is small (i.e.,for \( x \) nearly centered) is \[{\lambda }_{i} = \frac{1}{-t{f}_{i}\left( x\right) }\left( {1 + \frac{\nabla {f}_{i}{\left( x\right) }^{T}\Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}}}{-{f}_{i}\left( x\right) }}\right) ,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m.\] In this case,the vector \( x \) does not minimize \( L\left( {x,\lambda }\right) \) ,so there is no general formula for the dual function value \( g\left( \lambda \right) \) associated with \( \lambda \) . (If we have an analytical expression for the dual objective,however,we can simply evaluate \( g\left( \lambda \right) \) .) Verify that for a QCQP \[\text{ minimize }\;\left( {1/2}\right) {x}^{T}{P}_{0}x + {q}_{0}^{T}x + {r}_{0}\] \[\text{ subject to }\left( {1/2}\right) {x}^{T}{P}_{i}x + {q}_{i}^{T}x + {r}_{i} \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m\text{ , }\] the formula for \( \lambda \) yields a dual feasible point (i.e., \( \lambda \succcurlyeq 0 \) and \( L\left( {x,\lambda }\right) \) is bounded below) when \( \Delta {x}_{\mathrm{{nt}}} \) is sufficiently small.

We consider a convex-concave game with inequality constraints, subject to \[{\operatorname{minimize}}_{w}{\operatorname{maximize}}_{z}\;{f}_{0}\left( {w,z}\right)\] \[{\widetilde{f}}_{i}\left( z\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,\widetilde{m}.\] \( {f}_{i}\left( w\right) \leq 0,\;i = 1,\ldots ,m \) Here \( w \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is the variable associated with minimizing the objective,and \( z \in {\mathbf{R}}^{\widetilde{n}} \) is the variable associated with maximizing the objective. The constraint functions \( {f}_{i} \) and \( {\widetilde{f}}_{i} \) are convex and differentiable,and the objective function \( {f}_{0} \) is differentiable and convex-concave,i.e.,convex in \( w \) ,for each \( z \) ,and concave in \( z \) ,for each \( w \) . We assume for simplicity that \( \operatorname{dom}{f}_{0} = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times {\mathbf{R}}^{\widetilde{n}} \) . A solution or saddle-point for the game is a pair \( {w}^{ \star },{z}^{ \star } \) ,for which \[{f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star },z}\right) \leq {f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star },{z}^{ \star }}\right) \leq {f}_{0}\left( {w,{z}^{ \star }}\right)\] holds for every feasible \( w \) and \( z \) . (For background on convex-concave games and functions, see §5.4.3, §10.3.4 and exercises 3.14, 5.24, 5.25, 10.10, and 10.13.) In this exercise we show how to solve this game using an extension of the barrier method, and the infeasible start Newton method (see §10.3). (a) Let \( t > 0 \) . Explain why the function \[t{f}_{0}\left( {w,z}\right) - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\log \left( {-{f}_{i}\left( w\right) }\right) + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{\widetilde{m}}\log \left( {-{\widetilde{f}}_{i}\left( z\right) }\right)\] is convex-concave in \( \left( {w,z}\right) \) . We will assume that it has a unique saddle-point, \( \left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) \) ,which can be found using the infeasible start Newton method. (b) As in the barrier method for solving a convex optimization problem, we can derive a simple bound on the suboptimality of \( \left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) \) ,which depends only on the problem dimensions,and decreases to zero as \( t \) increases. Let \( W \) and \( Z \) denote the feasible sets for \( w \) and \( z \) , \[W = \left\{ {w \mid {f}_{i}\left( w\right) \leq 0,i = 1,\ldots ,m}\right\} ,\;Z = \left\{ {z \mid {\widetilde{f}}_{i}\left( z\right) \leq 0,i = 1,\ldots ,\widetilde{m}}\right\} .\] Show that \[{f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) \leq \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{w \in W}}{f}_{0}\left( {w,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) + \frac{m}{t}\] \[{f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) \geq \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{z \in Z}}{f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,z}\right) - \frac{\widetilde{m}}{t},\] and therefore \[\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{z \in Z}}{f}_{0}\left( {{w}^{ \star }\left( t\right) ,z}\right) - \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{w \in W}}{f}_{0}\left( {w,{z}^{ \star }\left( t\right) }\right) \leq \frac{m + \widetilde{m}}{t}.\] ## Self-concordance and complexity analysis 11.13 Self-concordance and negative entropy. pages.md: ## Numerical experiments 11.21 Log-Chebyshev approximation with bounds. We consider an approximation problem: find \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,that satisfies the variable bounds \( l \preccurlyeq x \preccurlyeq u \) ,and yields \( {Ax} \approx b \) ,where \( b \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) . You can assume that \( l \prec u \) ,and \( b \succ 0 \) (for reasons we explain below). We let \( {a}_{i}^{T} \) denote the \( i \) th row of the matrix \( A \) . We judge the approximation \( {Ax} \approx b \) by the maximum fractional deviation,which is \[\mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots ,n}}\max \left\{ {\left( {{a}_{i}^{T}x}\right) /{b}_{i},{b}_{i}/\left( {{a}_{i}^{T}x}\right) }\right\} = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots ,n}}\frac{\max \left\{ {{a}_{i}^{T}x,{b}_{i}}\right\} }{\min \left\{ {{a}_{i}^{T}x,{b}_{i}}\right\} },\] when \( {Ax} \succ 0 \) ; we define the maximum fractional deviation as \( \infty \) if \( {Ax} \nsucc 0 \) . The problem of minimizing the maximum fractional deviation is called the fractional Chebyshev approximation problem, or the logarithmic Chebyshev approximation problem, since it is equivalent to minimizing the objective \[\mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots ,n}}\left| {\log {a}_{i}^{T}x - \log {b}_{i}}\right| .\] (See also exercise 6.3, part (c).) (a) Formulate the fractional Chebyshev approximation problem (with variable bounds) as a convex optimization problem with twice differentiable objective and constraint functions. ## Appendix A Mathematical background

In this appendix we give a brief review of some basic concepts from analysis and linear algebra. The treatment is by no means complete, and is meant mostly to set out our notation.

### A.1 Norms

#### A.1.1 Inner product, Euclidean norm, and angle

The standard inner product on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,the set of real \( n \) -vectors,is given by

\[\langle x,y\rangle  = {x}^{T}y = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}\]

for \( x,y \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . In this book we use the notation \( {x}^{T}y \) ,instead of \( \langle x,y\rangle \) . The Euclidean norm,or \( {\ell }_{2} \) -norm,of a vector \( x \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is defined as

\[\parallel x{\parallel }_{2} = {\left( {x}^{T}x\right) }^{1/2} = {\left( {x}_{1}^{2} + \cdots  + {x}_{n}^{2}\right) }^{1/2}. \tag{A.1}\]

The Cauchy-Schwartz inequality states that \( \left| {{x}^{T}y}\right|  \leq  \parallel x{\parallel }_{2}\parallel y{\parallel }_{2} \) for any \( x,y \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . The (unsigned) angle between nonzero vectors \( x,y \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is defined as

\[L\left( {x,y}\right)  = {\cos }^{-1}\left( \frac{{x}^{T}y}{\parallel x{\parallel }_{2}\parallel y{\parallel }_{2}}\right) ,\]

where we take \( {\cos }^{-1}\left( u\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\pi }\right\rbrack \) . We say \( x \) and \( y \) are orthogonal if \( {x}^{T}y = 0 \) .

The standard inner product on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times  n} \) ,the set of \( m \times  n \) real matrices,is given by

\[\langle X,Y\rangle  = \operatorname{tr}\left( {{X}^{T}Y}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{X}_{ij}{Y}_{ij}\]

for \( X,Y \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times  n} \) . (Here \( \operatorname{tr} \) denotes trace of a matrix,i.e.,the sum of its diagonal elements.) We use the notation \( \operatorname{tr}\left( {{X}^{T}Y}\right) \) instead of \( \langle X,Y\rangle \) . Note that the inner product of two matrices is the inner product of the associated vectors,in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{mn} \) , obtained by listing the coefficients of the matrices in some order, such as row major.

(The \( {\ell }_{2} \) -norm of a matrix is a different norm; see §A.1.5.) The standard inner product on \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,the set of symmetric \( n \times n \) matrices,is given by \[\langle X,Y\rangle = \mathbf{{tr}}\left( {XY}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{X}_{ij}{Y}_{ij} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{ii}{Y}_{ii} + 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i < j}}{X}_{ij}{Y}_{ij}.\] #### A.1.2 Norms, distance, and unit ball A function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) with \( \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called a norm if - \( f \) is nonnegative: \( f\left( x\right) \geq 0 \) for all \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) - \( f \) is definite: \( f\left( x\right) = 0 \) only if \( x = 0 \) - \( f \) is homogeneous: \( f\left( {tx}\right) = \left| t\right| f\left( x\right) \) ,for all \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( t \in \mathbf{R} \) - \( f \) satisfies the triangle inequality: \( f\left( {x + y}\right) \leq f\left( x\right) + f\left( y\right) \) ,for all \( x,y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) We use the notation \( f\left( x\right) = \parallel x\parallel \) ,which is meant to suggest that a norm is a generalization of the absolute value on \( \mathbf{R} \) . When we specify a particular norm, we use the notation \( \parallel x{\parallel }_{\text{ symb }} \) ,where the subscript is a mnemonic to indicate which norm is meant. A norm is a measure of the length of a vector \( x \) ; we can measure the distance between two vectors \( x \) and \( y \) as the length of their difference,i.e., \[\operatorname{dist}\left( {x,y}\right) = \parallel x - y\parallel .\] We refer to \( \operatorname{dist}\left( {x,y}\right) \) as the distance between \( x \) and \( y \) ,in the norm \( \parallel \cdot \parallel \) . The set of all vectors with norm less than or equal to one, \[\mathcal{B} = \left\{ {x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \mid \parallel x\parallel \leq 1}\right\}\] is called the unit ball of the norm \( \parallel \cdot \parallel \) . The unit ball satisfies the following properties: - \( \mathcal{B} \) is symmetric about the origin,i.e., \( x \in \mathcal{B} \) if and only if \( - x \in \mathcal{B} \) - \( \mathcal{B} \) is convex - \( \mathcal{B} \) is closed,bounded,and has nonempty interior Conversely,if \( C \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is any set satisfying these three conditions,then it is the unit ball of a norm, which is given by \[\parallel x\parallel = {\left( \sup \{ t \geq 0 \mid tx \in C\} \right) }^{-1}.\]

pages.md: #### A.1.3 Examples The simplest example of a norm is the absolute value on \( \mathbf{R} \) . Another simple example is the Euclidean or \( {\ell }_{2} \) -norm on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,defined above in (A.1). Two other frequently used norms on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) are the sum-absolute-value,or \( {\ell }_{1} \) -norm,given by \[\parallel x{\parallel }_{1} = \left| {x}_{1}\right| + \cdots + \left| {x}_{n}\right| ,\] and the Chebyshev or \( {\ell }_{\infty } \) -norm,given by \[\parallel x{\parallel }_{\infty } = \max \left\{ {\left| {x}_{1}\right| ,\ldots ,\left| {x}_{n}\right| }\right\} .\] These three norms are part of a family parametrized by a constant traditionally denoted \( p \) ,with \( p \geq 1 \) : the \( {\ell }_{p} \) -norm is defined by \[\parallel x{\parallel }_{p} = {\left( {\left| {x}_{1}\right| }^{p} + \cdots + {\left| {x}_{n}\right| }^{p}\right) }^{1/p}.\] This yields the \( {\ell }_{1} \) -norm when \( p = 1 \) and the Euclidean norm when \( p = 2 \) . It is easy to show that for any \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , \[\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{p \rightarrow \infty }}\parallel x{\parallel }_{p} = \max \left\{ {\left| {x}_{1}\right| ,\ldots ,\left| {x}_{n}\right| }\right\}\] so the \( {\ell }_{\infty } \) -norm also fits in this family,as a limit. Another important family of norms are the quadratic norms. For \( P \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) ,we define the \( P \) -quadratic norm as \[\parallel x{\parallel }_{P} = {\left( {x}^{T}Px\right) }^{1/2} = {\begin{Vmatrix}{P}^{1/2}x\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}.\] The unit ball of a quadratic norm is an ellipsoid (and conversely, if the unit ball of a norm is an ellipsoid, the norm is a quadratic norm). Some common norms on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) are the Frobenius norm,defined above in (A.2), the sum-absolute-value norm, \[\parallel X{\parallel }_{\text{ sav }} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}\left| {X}_{ij}\right|\] and the maximum-absolute-value norm, \[\parallel X{\parallel }_{\operatorname{mav}} = \max \left\{ {\left| {X}_{ij}\right| \mid i = 1,\ldots ,m,j = 1,\ldots ,n}\right\} .\] We will encounter several other important norms of matrices in \( § \) A.1.5. #### A.1.4 Equivalence of norms Suppose that \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}} \) and \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{b}} \) are norms on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . A basic result of analysis is that there exist positive constants \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) such that,for all \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , \[\alpha \parallel x{\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}} \leq \parallel x{\parallel }_{\mathrm{b}} \leq \beta \parallel x{\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}}.\]

(We conclude that any norms on any finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent, but on infinite-dimensional vector spaces, the result need not hold.) Using convex analysis,we can give a more specific result: If \( \parallel \cdot \parallel \) is any norm on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,then there exists a quadratic norm \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{P} \) for which \[\parallel x{\parallel }_{P} \leq \parallel x\parallel \leq \sqrt{n}\parallel x{\parallel }_{P}\] holds for all \( x \) . In other words,any norm on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) can be uniformly approximated, within a factor of \( \sqrt{n} \) ,by a quadratic norm. (See \( §{8.4.1} \) .) #### A.1.5 Operator norms Suppose \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}} \) and \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{b}} \) are norms on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) and \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,respectively. We define the operator norm of \( X \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) ,induced by the norms \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}} \) and \( \parallel \cdot {\parallel }_{\mathrm{b}} \) ,as \[\parallel X{\parallel }_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{b}} = \sup \left\{ {\parallel {Xu}{\parallel }_{\mathrm{a}} \mid \parallel u{\parallel }_{\mathrm{b}} \leq 1}\right\} .\] (It can be shown that this defines a norm on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) .) pages.md: From the definition of dual norm we have the inequality \[{z}^{T}x \leq \parallel x\parallel \parallel z{\parallel }_{ * },\] which holds for all \( x \) and \( z \) . This inequality is tight,in the following sense: for any \( x \) there is a \( z \) for which the inequality holds with equality. (Similarly,for any \( z \) there is an \( x \) that gives equality.) The dual of the dual norm is the original norm: we have \( \parallel x{\parallel }_{* * } = \parallel x\parallel \) for all \( x \) . (This need not hold in infinite-dimensional vector spaces.) The dual of the Euclidean norm is the Euclidean norm, since \[\sup \left\{ {{z}^{T}x \mid \parallel x{\parallel }_{2} \leq 1}\right\} = \parallel z{\parallel }_{2}.\] (This follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; for nonzero \( z \) ,the value of \( x \) that maximizes \( {z}^{T}x \) over \( \parallel x{\parallel }_{2} \leq 1 \) is \( z/\parallel z{\parallel }_{2} \) .) The dual of the \( {\ell }_{\infty } \) -norm is the \( {\ell }_{1} \) -norm: \[\sup \left\{ {{z}^{T}x \mid \parallel x{\parallel }_{\infty } \leq 1}\right\} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left| {z}_{i}\right| = \parallel z{\parallel }_{1},\] and the dual of the \( {\ell }_{1} \) -norm is the \( {\ell }_{\infty } \) -norm. More generally,the dual of the \( {\ell }_{p} \) -norm is the \( {\ell }_{q} \) -norm,where \( q \) satisfies \( 1/p + 1/q = 1 \) ,i.e., \( q = p/\left( {p - 1}\right) \) . As another example,consider the \( {\ell }_{2} \) - or spectral norm on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) . The associated dual norm is \[\parallel Z{\parallel }_{2 * } = \sup \left\{ {\operatorname{tr}\left( {{Z}^{T}X}\right) \mid \parallel X{\parallel }_{2} \leq 1}\right\} ,\] which turns out to be the sum of the singular values, \[\parallel Z{\parallel }_{2 * } = {\sigma }_{1}\left( Z\right) + \cdots + {\sigma }_{r}\left( Z\right) = \operatorname{tr}{\left( {Z}^{T}Z\right) }^{1/2},\] where \( r = \operatorname{rank}Z \) . This norm is sometimes called the nuclear norm. ### A.2 Analysis #### A.2.1 Open and closed sets An element \( x \in C \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called an interior point of \( C \) if there exists an \( \epsilon > 0 \) for which \[\left\{ {y \mid \parallel y - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq \epsilon }\right\} \subseteq C,\] i.e.,there exists a ball centered at \( x \) that lies entirely in \( C \) . The set of all points interior to \( C \) is called the interior of \( C \) and is denoted int \( C \) . (Since all norms on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) are equivalent to the Euclidean norm,all norms generate the same set of interior points.) A set \( C \) is open if int \( C = C \) ,i.e.,every point in \( C \) is an interior point. A set \( C \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is closed if its complement \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \smallsetminus C = \left\{ {x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \mid x \notin C}\right\} \) is open.

pages.md: The closure of a set \( C \) is defined as \[\operatorname{cl}C = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \smallsetminus \operatorname{int}\left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n} \smallsetminus C}\right) ,\] i.e.,the complement of the interior of the complement of \( C \) . A point \( x \) is in the closure of \( C \) if for every \( \epsilon > 0 \) ,there is a \( y \in C \) with \( \parallel x - y{\parallel }_{2} \leq \epsilon \) . We can also describe closed sets and the closure in terms of convergent sequences and limit points. A set \( C \) is closed if and only if it contains the limit point of every convergent sequence in it. In other words,if \( {x}_{1},{x}_{2},\ldots \) converges to \( x \) ,and \( {x}_{i} \in C \) , then \( x \in C \) . The closure of \( C \) is the set of all limit points of convergent sequences in \( C \) . The boundary of the set \( C \) is defined as \[\operatorname{bd}C = \operatorname{cl}C \smallsetminus \operatorname{int}C.\] A boundary point \( x \) (i.e.,a point \( x \in \operatorname{bd}C \) ) satisfies the following property: For all \( \epsilon > 0 \) ,there exists \( y \in C \) and \( z \notin C \) with \[\parallel y - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq \epsilon ,\;\parallel z - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq \epsilon ,\] i.e.,there exist arbitrarily close points in \( C \) ,and also arbitrarily close points not in \( C \) . We can characterize closed and open sets in terms of the boundary operation: \( C \) is closed if it contains its boundary,i.e.,bd \( C \subseteq C \) . It is open if it contains no boundary points,i.e., \( C \cap \operatorname{bd}C = \varnothing \) . #### A.2.2 Supremum and infimum Suppose \( C \subseteq \mathbf{R} \) . A number \( a \) is an upper bound on \( C \) if for each \( x \in C,x \leq a \) . The set of upper bounds on a set \( C \) is either empty (in which case we say \( C \) is unbounded above),all of \( \mathbf{R} \) (only when \( C = \varnothing \) ),or a closed infinite interval \( \lbrack b,\infty ) \) . The number \( b \) is called the least upper bound or supremum of the set \( C \) ,and is denoted sup \( C \) . We take sup \( \varnothing = - \infty \) ,and sup \( C = \infty \) if \( C \) is unbounded above. When \( \sup C \in C \) ,we say the supremum of \( C \) is attained or achieved. When the set \( C \) is finite, \( \sup C \) is the maximum of its elements. Some authors use the notation \( \max C \) to denote supremum,when it is attained,but we follow standard mathematical convention,using \( \max C \) only when the set \( C \) is finite. We define lower bound,and infimum,in a similar way. A number \( a \) is a lower bound on \( C \subseteq \mathbf{R} \) if for each \( x \in C,a \leq x \) . The infimum (or greatest lower bound) of a set \( C \subseteq \mathbf{R} \) is defined as inf \( C = - \sup \left( {-C}\right) \) . When \( C \) is finite,the infimum is the minimum of its elements. We take inf \( \varnothing = \infty \) ,and inf \( C = - \infty \) if \( C \) is unbounded below, i.e., has no lower bound.

pages.md: ### A.3 Functions #### A.3.1 Function notation Our notation for functions is mostly standard, with one exception. When we write \[f : A \rightarrow B\] we mean that \( f \) is a function on the set \( \operatorname{dom}f \subseteq A \) into the set \( B \) ; in particular we can have \( \operatorname{dom}f \) a proper subset of the set \( A \) . Thus the notation \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) means that \( f \) maps (some) \( n \) -vectors into \( m \) -vectors; it does not mean that \( f\left( x\right) \) is defined for every \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . This convention is similar to function declarations in computer languages. Specifying the data types of the input and output arguments of a function gives the syntax of that function; it does not guarantee that any input argument with the specified data type is valid. As an example consider the function \( f : {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,given by \[f\left( X\right) = \log \det X, \tag{A.3}\] with \( \operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . The notation \( f : {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) specifies the syntax of \( f \) : it takes as argument a symmetric \( n \times n \) matrix,and returns a real number. The notation dom \( f = {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) specifies which symmetric \( n \times n \) matrices are valid input arguments for \( f \) (i.e.,only positive definite ones). The formula (A.3) specifies what \( f\left( X\right) \) is, for \( X \in \operatorname{dom}f \) . #### A.3.2 Continuity A function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is continuous at \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) if for all \( \epsilon > 0 \) there exists a \( \delta \) such that \[y \in \operatorname{dom}f,\;\parallel y - x{\parallel }_{2} \leq \delta \Rightarrow \parallel f\left( y\right) - f\left( x\right) {\parallel }_{2} \leq \epsilon .\] Continuity can be described in terms of limits: whenever the sequence \( {x}_{1},{x}_{2},\ldots \) in \( \operatorname{dom}f \) converges to a point \( x \in \operatorname{dom}f \) ,the sequence \( f\left( {x}_{1}\right) ,f\left( {x}_{2}\right) ,\ldots \) converges to \( f\left( x\right) \) ,i.e., \[\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow \infty }}f\left( {x}_{i}\right) = f\left( {\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow \infty }}{x}_{i}}\right) .\] A function \( f \) is continuous if it is continuous at every point in its domain. #### A.3.3 Closed functions A function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) is said to be closed if,for each \( \alpha \in \mathbf{R} \) ,the sublevel set \[\{ x \in \operatorname{dom}f \mid f\left( x\right) \leq \alpha \}\] is closed. This is equivalent to the condition that the epigraph of \( f \) , \[\text{ epi }f = \left\{ {\left( {x,t}\right) \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \mid x \in \operatorname{dom}f,f\left( x\right) \leq t}\right\} \text{ , }\]

The function \( f \) is differentiable at \( x \) if there exists a matrix \( {Df}\left( x\right) \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) that satisfies \[\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{z \in \operatorname{dom}f,z \neq x,z \rightarrow x}}\frac{\parallel f\left( z\right) - f\left( x\right) - {Df}\left( x\right) \left( {z - x}\right) {\parallel }_{2}}{\parallel z - x{\parallel }_{2}} = 0, \tag{A.4}\] in which case we refer to \( {Df}\left( x\right) \) as the derivative (or Jacobian) of \( f \) at \( x \) . (There can be at most one matrix that satisfies (A.4).) The function \( f \) is differentiable if dom \( f \) is open,and it is differentiable at every point in its domain. The affine function of \( z \) given by \[f\left( x\right) + {Df}\left( x\right) \left( {z - x}\right)\] is called the first-order approximation of \( f \) at (or near) \( x \) . Evidently this function agrees with \( f \) at \( z = x \) ; when \( z \) is close to \( x \) ,this affine function is very close to \( f \) . The derivative can be found by deriving the first-order approximation of the function \( f \) at \( x \) (i.e.,the matrix \( {Df}\left( x\right) \) that satisfies (A.4)),or from partial derivatives: \[{Df}{\left( x\right) }_{ij} = \frac{\partial {f}_{i}\left( x\right) }{\partial {x}_{j}},\;i = 1,\ldots ,m,\;j = 1,\ldots ,n.\]

Its transpose is called the gradient of the function: \[\nabla f\left( x\right) = {Df}{\left( x\right) }^{T},\] which is a (column) vector,i.e.,in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Its components are the partial derivatives of \( f \) : \[\nabla f{\left( x\right) }_{i} = \frac{\partial f\left( x\right) }{\partial {x}_{i}},\;i = 1,\ldots ,n.\] The first-order approximation of \( f \) at a point \( x \in \) int dom \( f \) can be expressed as (the affine function of \( z \) ) \[f\left( x\right) + \nabla f{\left( x\right) }^{T}\left( {z - x}\right) .\] ## Examples As a simple example consider the quadratic function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) , \[f\left( x\right) = \left( {1/2}\right) {x}^{T}{Px} + {q}^{T}x + r,\] where \( P \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n},q \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,and \( r \in \mathbf{R} \) . Its derivative at \( x \) is the row vector \( {Df}\left( x\right) = \; {x}^{T}P + {q}^{T} \) ,and its gradient is \[\nabla f\left( x\right) = {Px} + q.\] As a more interesting example,we consider the function \( f : {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R} \) ,given by \[f\left( X\right) = \log \det X,\;\operatorname{dom}f = {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n}.\] One (tedious) way to find the gradient of \( f \) is to introduce a basis for \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,find the gradient of the associated function,and finally translate the result back to \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . Instead,we will directly find the first-order approximation of \( f \) at \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . Let \( Z \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) be close to \( X \) ,and let \( {\Delta X} = Z - X \) (which is assumed to be small). We have \[\log \det Z = \log \det \left( {X + {\Delta X}}\right)\] \[= \log \det \left( {{X}^{1/2}\left( {I + {X}^{-1/2}{\Delta X}{X}^{-1/2}}\right) {X}^{1/2}}\right)\] \[= \log \det X + \log \det \left( {I + {X}^{-1/2}{\Delta X}{X}^{-1/2}}\right)\] \[= \log \det X + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log \left( {1 + {\lambda }_{i}}\right) ,\] where \( {\lambda }_{i} \) is the \( i \) th eigenvalue of \( {X}^{-1/2}{\Delta X}{X}^{-1/2} \) . Now we use the fact that \( {\Delta X} \) is small,which implies \( {\lambda }_{i} \) are small,so to first order we have \( \log \left( {1 + {\lambda }_{i}}\right) \approx {\lambda }_{i} \) . Using this first-order approximation in the expression above, we get \[\log \det Z \approx \log \det X + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\] \[= \log \det X + \operatorname{tr}\left( {{X}^{-1/2}{\Delta X}{X}^{-1/2}}\right)\] \[= \log \det X + \operatorname{tr}\left( {{X}^{-1}{\Delta X}}\right)\] \[= \log \det X + \operatorname{tr}\left( {{X}^{-1}\left( {Z - X}\right) }\right) ,\]

Simply working out the partial derivatives yields \[{\nabla }^{2}h\left( x\right) = {g}^{\prime }\left( {f\left( x\right) }\right) {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) + {g}^{\prime \prime }\left( {f\left( x\right) }\right) \nabla f\left( x\right) \nabla f{\left( x\right) }^{T}. \tag{A.8}\] ## Composition with affine function Suppose \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbf{R},A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times m} \) ,and \( b \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . pages.md: \[\mathcal{R}\left( A\right) = \left\{ {{Ax} \mid x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n}}\right\} .\] The range \( \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) \) is a subspace of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) ,i.e.,it is itself a vector space. Its dimension is the rank of \( A \) ,denoted rank \( A \) . The rank of \( A \) can never be greater than the minimum of \( m \) and \( n \) . We say \( A \) has full rank if \( \operatorname{rank}A = \min \{ m,n\} \) . The nullspace (or kernel) of \( A \) ,denoted \( \mathcal{N}\left( A\right) \) ,is the set of all vectors \( x \) mapped into zero by \( A \) : \[\mathcal{N}\left( A\right) = \{ x \mid {Ax} = 0\} .\] The nullspace is a subspace of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . ## Orthogonal decomposition induced by \( A \) If \( \mathcal{V} \) is a subspace of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ,its orthogonal complement,denoted \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ \bot } \) ,is defined as \[{\mathcal{V}}^{ \bot } = \left\{ {x \mid {z}^{T}x = 0\text{ for all }z \in \mathcal{V}}\right\}\] (As one would expect of a complement,we have \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ \bot \bot } = \mathcal{V} \) .) A basic result of linear algebra is that,for any \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) ,we have \[\mathcal{N}\left( A\right) = \mathcal{R}{\left( {A}^{T}\right) }^{ \bot }.\] (Applying the result to \( {A}^{T} \) we also have \( \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) = \mathcal{N}{\left( {A}^{T}\right) }^{ \bot } \) .) This result is often stated as \[\mathcal{N}\left( A\right) \overset{ \bot }{ \oplus }\mathcal{R}\left( {A}^{T}\right) = {\mathbf{R}}^{n}. \tag{A.9}\] Here the symbol \( \dot{ \oplus } \) refers to orthogonal direct sum,i.e.,the sum of two subspaces that are orthogonal. The decomposition (A.9) of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called the orthogonal decomposition induced by \( A \) . #### A.5.2 Symmetric eigenvalue decomposition Suppose \( A \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,i.e., \( A \) is a real symmetric \( n \times n \) matrix. Then \( A \) can be factored as \[A = {Q\Lambda }{Q}^{T}, \tag{A.10}\] where \( Q \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is orthogonal,i.e.,satisfies \( {Q}^{T}Q = I \) ,and \( \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}\left( {{\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n}}\right) \) . The (real) numbers \( {\lambda }_{i} \) are the eigenvalues of \( A \) ,and are the roots of the characteristic polynomial \( \det \left( {{sI} - A}\right) \) . The columns of \( Q \) form an orthonormal set of eigenvectors of \( A \) . The factorization (A.10) is called the spectral decomposition or (symmetric) eigenvalue decomposition of \( A \) . We order the eigenvalues as \( {\lambda }_{1} \geq {\lambda }_{2} \geq \cdots \geq {\lambda }_{n} \) . We use the notation \( {\lambda }_{i}\left( A\right) \) to refer to the \( i \) th largest eigenvalue of \( A \in \mathbf{S} \) . We usually write the largest or maximum eigenvalue as \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( A\right) = {\lambda }_{\max }\left( A\right) \) ,and the least or minimum eigenvalue as \( {\lambda }_{n}\left( A\right) = {\lambda }_{\min }\left( A\right) . \)

pages.md: The determinant and trace can be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues, \[\det A = \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i},\;\operatorname{tr}A = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}\] as can the spectral and Frobenius norms, \[\parallel A{\parallel }_{2} = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots ,n}}\left| {\lambda }_{i}\right| = \max \left\{ {{\lambda }_{1}, - {\lambda }_{n}}\right\} ,\;\parallel A{\parallel }_{F} = {\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}^{2}\right) }^{1/2}.\] ## Definiteness and matrix inequalities The largest and smallest eigenvalues satisfy \[{\lambda }_{\max }\left( A\right) = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \neq 0}}\frac{{x}^{T}{Ax}}{{x}^{T}x},\;{\lambda }_{\min }\left( A\right) = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \neq 0}}\frac{{x}^{T}{Ax}}{{x}^{T}x}.\] In particular,for any \( x \) ,we have \[{\lambda }_{\min }\left( A\right) {x}^{T}x \leq {x}^{T}{Ax} \leq {\lambda }_{\max }\left( A\right) {x}^{T}x,\] with both inequalities tight for (different) choices of \( x \) . A matrix \( A \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) is called positive definite if for all \( x \neq 0,{x}^{T}{Ax} > 0 \) . We denote this as \( A \succ 0 \) . By the inequality above,we see that \( A \succ 0 \) if and only all its eigenvalues are positive,i.e., \( {\lambda }_{\min }\left( A\right) > 0 \) . If \( - A \) is positive definite,we say \( A \) is negative definite,which we write as \( A \prec 0 \) . We use \( {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) to denote the set of positive definite matrices in \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . If \( A \) satisfies \( {x}^{T}{Ax} \geq 0 \) for all \( x \) ,we say that \( A \) is positive semidefinite or nonnegative definite. If \( - A \) is nonnegative definite,i.e.,if \( {x}^{T}{Ax} \leq 0 \) for all \( x \) ,we say that \( A \) is negative semidefinite or nonpositive definite. We use \( {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n} \) to denote the set of nonnegative definite matrices in \( {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) . For \( A,B \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,we use \( A \prec B \) to mean \( B - A \succ 0 \) ,and so on. These inequalities are called matrix inequalities, or generalized inequalities associated with the positive semidefinite cone. ## Symmetric squareroot Let \( A \in {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n} \) ,with eigenvalue decomposition \( A = Q\operatorname{diag}\left( {{\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n}}\right) {Q}^{T} \) . We define the (symmetric) squareroot of \( A \) as \[{A}^{1/2} = Q\operatorname{diag}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{1/2},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n}^{1/2}}\right) {Q}^{T}.\] The squareroot \( {A}^{1/2} \) is the unique symmetric positive semidefinite solution of the equation \( {X}^{2} = A \) . #### A.5.3 Generalized eigenvalue decomposition The generalized eigenvalues of a pair of symmetric matrices \( \left( {A,B}\right) \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \times {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) are defined as the roots of the polynomial \( \det \left( {{sB} - A}\right) \) .

pages.md: We are usually interested in matrix pairs with \( B \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) . In this case the generalized eigenvalues are also the eigenvalues of \( {B}^{-1/2}A{B}^{-1/2} \) (which are real). As with the standard eigenvalue decomposition, we order the generalized eigenvalues in nonincreasing order,as \( {\lambda }_{1} \geq {\lambda }_{2} \geq \cdots \geq {\lambda }_{n} \) ,and denote the maximum generalized eigenvalue by \( {\lambda }_{\max }\left( {A,B}\right) \) . When \( B \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + }^{n} \) ,the pair of matrices can be factored as \[A = {V\Lambda }{V}^{T},\;B = V{V}^{T}, \tag{A.11}\] where \( V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is nonsingular,and \( \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}\left( {{\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n}}\right) \) ,where \( {\lambda }_{i} \) are the generalized eigenvalues of the pair \( \left( {A,B}\right) \) . The decomposition (A.11) is called the generalized eigenvalue decomposition. The generalized eigenvalue decomposition is related to the standard eigenvalue decomposition of the matrix \( {B}^{-1/2}A{B}^{-1/2} \) . If \( {Q\Lambda }{Q}^{T} \) is the eigenvalue decomposition of \( {B}^{-1/2}A{B}^{-1/2} \) ,then (A.11) holds with \( V = {B}^{1/2}Q \) . #### A.5.4 Singular value decomposition Suppose \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) with rank \( A = r \) . Then \( A \) can be factored as \[A = {U\sum }{V}^{T}, \tag{A.12}\] where \( U \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times r} \) satisfies \( {U}^{T}U = I,V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times r} \) satisfies \( {V}^{T}V = I \) ,and \( \sum = \; \operatorname{diag}\left( {{\sigma }_{1},\ldots ,{\sigma }_{r}}\right) \) ,with \[{\sigma }_{1} \geq {\sigma }_{2} \geq \cdots \geq {\sigma }_{r} > 0\] The factorization (A.12) is called the singular value decomposition (SVD) of \( A \) . The columns of \( U \) are called left singular vectors of \( A \) ,the columns of \( V \) are right singular vectors,and the numbers \( {\sigma }_{i} \) are the singular values. The singular value decomposition can be written \[A = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{r}{\sigma }_{i}{u}_{i}{v}_{i}^{T}\] where \( {u}_{i} \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) are the left singular vectors,and \( {v}_{i} \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) are the right singular vectors. The singular value decomposition of a matrix \( A \) is closely related to the eigenvalue decomposition of the (symmetric,nonnegative definite) matrix \( {A}^{T}A \) . Using (A.12) we can write \[{A}^{T}A = V{\sum }^{2}{V}^{T} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} V & \widetilde{V} \end{array}\right\rbrack \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} {\sum }^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{matrix}\right\rbrack {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} V & \widetilde{V} \end{array}\right\rbrack }^{T},\] where \( \widetilde{V} \) is any matrix for which \( \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} V & \widetilde{V} \end{array}\right\rbrack \) is orthogonal. The righthand expression is the eigenvalue decomposition of \( {A}^{T}A \) ,so we conclude that its nonzero eigenvalues are the singular values of \( A \) squared,and the associated eigenvectors of \( {A}^{T}A \) are the right singular vectors of \( A \) . A similar analysis of \( A{A}^{T} \) shows that its nonzero eigenvalues are also the squares of the singular values of \( A \) ,and the associated eigenvectors are the left singular vectors of \( A \) .

pages.md: The first or largest singular value is also written as \( {\sigma }_{\max }\left( A\right) \) . It can be expressed as \[{\sigma }_{\max }\left( A\right) = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x,y \neq 0}}\frac{{x}^{T}{Ay}}{\parallel x{\parallel }_{2}\parallel y{\parallel }_{2}} = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \neq 0}}\frac{\parallel {Ay}{\parallel }_{2}}{\parallel y{\parallel }_{2}}.\] The righthand expression shows that the maximum singular value is the \( {\ell }_{2} \) operator norm of \( A \) . The minimum singular value of \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) is given by \[{\sigma }_{\min }\left( A\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {\sigma }_{r}\left( A\right) & r = \min \{ m,n\} \\ 0 & r < \min \{ m,n\} , \end{array}\right.\] which is positive if and only if \( A \) is full rank. The singular values of a symmetric matrix are the absolute values of its nonzero eigenvalues, sorted into descending order. The singular values of a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix are the same as its nonzero eigenvalues. The condition number of a nonsingular \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) ,denoted \( \operatorname{cond}\left( A\right) \) or \( \kappa \left( A\right) \) , is defined as \[\operatorname{cond}\left( A\right) = \parallel A{\parallel }_{2}{\begin{Vmatrix}{A}^{-1}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2} = {\sigma }_{\max }\left( A\right) /{\sigma }_{\min }\left( A\right) .\] ## Pseudo-inverse Let \( A = {U\sum }{V}^{T} \) be the singular value decomposition of \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) ,with rank \( A = \; r \) . We define the pseudo-inverse or Moore-Penrose inverse of \( A \) as \[{A}^{ \dagger } = V{\sum }^{-1}{U}^{T} \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times m}.\] Alternative expressions are \[{A}^{ \dagger } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\epsilon \rightarrow 0}}{\left( {A}^{T}A + \epsilon I\right) }^{-1}{A}^{T} = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\epsilon \rightarrow 0}}{A}^{T}{\left( A{A}^{T} + \epsilon I\right) }^{-1},\] where the limits are taken with \( \epsilon > 0 \) ,which ensures that the inverses in the expressions exist. If \( \operatorname{rank}A = n \) ,then \( {A}^{ \dagger } = {\left( {A}^{T}A\right) }^{-1}{A}^{T} \) . If \( \operatorname{rank}A = m \) ,then \( {A}^{ \dagger } = {A}^{T}{\left( A{A}^{T}\right) }^{-1} \) . If \( A \) is square and nonsingular,then \( {A}^{ \dagger } = {A}^{-1} \) . The pseudo-inverse comes up in problems involving least-squares, minimum norm,quadratic minimization,and (Euclidean) projection. For example, \( {A}^{ \dagger }b \) is a solution of the least-squares problem \[\text{ minimize }\parallel {Ax} - b{\parallel }_{2}^{2}\] in general. When the solution is not unique, \( {A}^{ \dagger }b \) gives the solution with minimum (Euclidean) norm. As another example,the matrix \( A{A}^{ \dagger } = U{U}^{T} \) gives (Euclidean) projection on \( \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) \) . The matrix \( {A}^{ \dagger }A = V{V}^{T} \) gives (Euclidean) projection on \( \mathcal{R}\left( {A}^{T}\right) \) . The optimal value \( {p}^{ \star } \) of the (general,nonconvex) quadratic optimization problem \[\text{ minimize }\left( {1/2}\right) {x}^{T}{Px} + {q}^{T}x + r\text{ , }\] where \( P \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,can be expressed as \[{p}^{ \star } = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} - \left( {1/2}\right) {q}^{T}{P}^{ \dagger }q + r & P \succcurlyeq 0,\;q \in \mathcal{R}\left( P\right) \\ - \infty & \text{ otherwise. } \end{array}\right.\] (This generalizes the expression \( {p}^{ \star } = - \left( {1/2}\right) {q}^{T}{P}^{-1}q + r \) ,valid for \( P \succ 0 \) .)

pages.md: #### A.5.5 Schur complement Consider a matrix \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) partitioned as \[X = \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} A & B \\ {B}^{T} & C \end{matrix}\right\rbrack\] where \( A \in {\mathbf{S}}^{k} \) . If \( \det A \neq 0 \) ,the matrix \[S = C - {B}^{T}{A}^{-1}B\] is called the Schur complement of \( A \) in \( X \) . Schur complements arise in several contexts, and appear in many important formulas and theorems. For example, we have \[\det X = \det A\det S.\] ## Inverse of block matrix The Schur complement comes up in solving linear equations, by eliminating one block of variables. We start with \[\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} A & B \\ {B}^{T} & C \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array}\right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} u \\ v \end{array}\right\rbrack\] and assume that \( \det A \neq 0 \) . If we eliminate \( x \) from the top block equation and substitute it into the bottom block equation,we obtain \( v = {B}^{T}{A}^{-1}u + {Sy} \) ,so \[y = {S}^{-1}\left( {v - {B}^{T}{A}^{-1}u}\right) .\] Substituting this into the first equation yields \[x = \left( {{A}^{-1} + {A}^{-1}B{S}^{-1}{B}^{T}{A}^{-1}}\right) u - {A}^{-1}B{S}^{-1}v.\] We can express these two equations as a formula for the inverse of a block matrix: \[{\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} A & B \\ {B}^{T} & C \end{matrix}\right\rbrack }^{-1} = \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} {A}^{-1} + {A}^{-1}B{S}^{-1}{B}^{T}{A}^{-1} & - {A}^{-1}B{S}^{-1} \\ - {S}^{-1}{B}^{T}{A}^{-1} & {S}^{-1} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack .\] In particular,we see that the Schur complement is the inverse of the 2,2 block entry of the inverse of \( X \) . ## Minimization and definiteness The Schur complement arises when you minimize a quadratic form over some of the variables. Suppose \( A \succ 0 \) ,and consider the minimization problem \[\text{ minimize }{u}^{T}{Au} + 2{v}^{T}{B}^{T}u + {v}^{T}{Cv} \tag{A.13}\] with variable \( u \) . The solution is \( u = - {A}^{-1}{Bv} \) ,and the optimal value is \[\mathop{\inf }\limits_{u}{\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} u \\ v \end{matrix}\right\rbrack }^{T}\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} A & B \\ {B}^{T} & C \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} u \\ v \end{matrix}\right\rbrack = {v}^{T}{Sv}. \tag{A.14}\] From this we can derive the following characterizations of positive definiteness or semidefiniteness of the block matrix \( X \) : - \( X \succ 0 \) if and only if \( A \succ 0 \) and \( S \succ 0 \) . - If \( A \succ 0 \) ,then \( X \succcurlyeq 0 \) if and only if \( S \succcurlyeq 0 \) .

pages.md: ## Schur complement with singular \( A \) Some Schur complement results have generalizations to the case when \( A \) is singular, although the details are more complicated. As an example,if \( A \succcurlyeq 0 \) and \( {Bv} \in \; \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) \) ,then the quadratic minimization problem (A.13) (with variable \( u \) ) is solvable, and has optimal value \[{v}^{T}\left( {C - {B}^{T}{A}^{ \dagger }B}\right) v\] where \( {A}^{ \dagger } \) is the pseudo-inverse of \( A \) . The problem is unbounded if \( {Bv} \notin \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) \) or if \( A \nsucceq 0 \) . The range condition \( {Bv} \in \mathcal{R}\left( A\right) \) can also be expressed as \( \left( {I - A{A}^{ \dagger }}\right) {Bv} = 0 \) , so we have the following characterization of positive semidefiniteness of the block matrix \( X \) : \[X \succcurlyeq 0 \Leftrightarrow A \succcurlyeq 0,\;\left( {I - A{A}^{ \dagger }}\right) B = 0,\;C - {B}^{T}{A}^{ \dagger }B \succcurlyeq 0.\] Here the matrix \( C - {B}^{T}{A}^{ \dagger }B \) serves as a generalization of the Schur complement, when \( A \) is singular.

The first result is that strong duality holds for problem (B.1) and its Lagrange dual (B.2), provided Slater's constraint qualification is satisfied, i.e., there exists an \( x \) with \( {x}^{T}{A}_{1}x + 2{b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} < 0 \) . In other words,if (B.1) is strictly feasible,the optimal values of (B.1) and (B.2) are equal. (A proof is given in §B.4.) ## Relaxation interpretation The dual of the SDP (B.2) is \[\text{ minimize }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{0}X}\right) + 2{b}_{0}^{T}x + {c}_{0}\] \[\text{ subject to }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{1}X}\right) + 2{b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} \leq 0 \tag{B.3}\] \[\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} X & x \\ {x}^{T} & 1 \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \succcurlyeq 0\] an SDP with variables \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n},x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . This dual SDP has an interesting interpretation in terms of the original problem (B.1). We first note that (B.1) is equivalent to \[\text{ minimize }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{0}X}\right) + 2{b}_{0}^{T}x + {c}_{0}\] \[\text{ subject to }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{1}X}\right) + 2{b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} \leq 0 \tag{B.4}\] \[X = x{x}^{T}.\] In this formulation we express the quadratic terms \( {x}^{T}{A}_{i}x \) as \( \operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{i}x{x}^{T}}\right) \) ,and then introduce a new variable \( X = x{x}^{T} \) . Problem (B.4) has a linear objective function, one linear inequality constraint,and a nonlinear equality constraint \( X = x{x}^{T} \) . The next step is to replace the equality constraint by an inequality \( X \succcurlyeq x{x}^{T} \) : \[\text{ minimize }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{0}X}\right) + {b}_{0}^{T}x + {c}_{0}\] \[\text{ subject to }\operatorname{tr}\left( {{A}_{1}X}\right) + {b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} \leq 0 \tag{B.5}\] \[X \succcurlyeq x{x}^{T}.\] This problem is called a relaxation of (B.4), since we have replaced one of the constraints with a looser constraint. Finally we note that the inequality in (B.5) can be expressed as a linear matrix inequality by using a Schur complement, which gives (B.3). A number of interesting facts follow immediately from this interpretation of (B.3) as a relaxation of (B.1). First, it is obvious that the optimal value of (B.3) is less than or equal to the optimal value of (B.1), since we minimize the same objective function over a larger set. Second,we can conclude that if \( X = x{x}^{T} \) at the optimum of (B.3),then \( x \) must be optimal in (B.1). Combining the result above, that strong duality holds between (B.1) and (B.2) (if (B.1) is strictly feasible), with strong duality between the dual SDPs (B.2) and (B.3), we conclude that strong duality holds between the original, nonconvex quadratic problem (B.1), and the SDP relaxation (B.3), provided (B.1) is strictly feasible.

pages.md: ### B.2 The S-procedure The next result is a theorem of alternatives for a pair of (nonconvex) quadratic inequalities. Let \( {A}_{1},{A}_{2} \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n},{b}_{1},{b}_{2} \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n},{c}_{1},{c}_{2} \in \mathbf{R} \) ,and suppose there exists an \( \widehat{x} \) with \[{\widehat{x}}^{T}{A}_{2}\widehat{x} + 2{b}_{2}^{T}\widehat{x} + {c}_{2} < 0.\] Then there exists an \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) satisfying \[{x}^{T}{A}_{1}x + 2{b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} < 0,\;{x}^{T}{A}_{2}x + 2{b}_{2}^{T}x + {c}_{2} \leq 0, \tag{B.6}\] if and only if there exists no \( \lambda \) such that \[\lambda \geq 0,\;\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {A}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}^{T} & {c}_{1} \end{array}\right\rbrack + \lambda \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {A}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}^{T} & {c}_{2} \end{array}\right\rbrack \succcurlyeq 0. \tag{B.7}\] In other words, (B.6) and (B.7) are strong alternatives. This result is readily shown to be equivalent to the result from §B.1, and a proof is given in §B.4. Here we point out that the two inequality systems are clearly weak alternatives, since (B.6) and (B.7) together lead to a contradiction: \[0 \leq {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ 1 \end{array}\right\rbrack }^{T}\left( {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {A}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}^{T} & {c}_{1} \end{array}\right\rbrack + \lambda \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {A}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}^{T} & {c}_{2} \end{array}\right\rbrack }\right) \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ 1 \end{array}\right\rbrack\] \[= {x}^{T}{A}_{1}x + 2{b}_{1}^{T}x + {c}_{1} + \lambda \left( {{x}^{T}{A}_{2}x + 2{b}_{2}^{T}x + {c}_{2}}\right)\] \[< 0\text{ . }\] This theorem of alternatives is sometimes called the \( S \) -procedure,and is usually stated in the following form: the implication \[{x}^{T}{F}_{1}x + 2{g}_{1}^{T}x + {h}_{1} \leq 0 \Rightarrow {x}^{T}{F}_{2}x + 2{g}_{2}^{T}x + {h}_{2} \leq 0,\] where \( {F}_{i} \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n},{g}_{i} \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n},{h}_{i} \in \mathbf{R} \) ,holds if and only if there exists a \( \lambda \) such that \[\lambda \geq 0,\;\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {F}_{2} & {g}_{2} \\ {g}_{2}^{T} & {h}_{2} \end{array}\right\rbrack \preccurlyeq \lambda \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {F}_{1} & {g}_{1} \\ {g}_{1}^{T} & {h}_{1} \end{array}\right\rbrack\] provided there exists a point \( \widehat{x} \) with \( {\widehat{x}}^{T}{F}_{1}\widehat{x} + 2{g}_{1}^{T}\widehat{x} + {h}_{1} < 0 \) . (Note that sufficiency is clear.) Example B.1 Ellipsoid containment. An ellipsoid \( \mathcal{E} \subseteq {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with nonempty interior can be represented as the sublevel set of a quadratic function, --- \[\mathcal{E} = \left\{ {x \mid {x}^{T}{Fx} + 2{g}^{T}x + h \leq 0}\right\} ,\] where \( F \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + } \) and \( h - {g}^{T}{F}^{-1}g < 0 \) . Suppose \( \widetilde{\mathcal{E}} \) is another ellipsoid with similar representation, \[\widetilde{\mathcal{E}} = \left\{ {x \mid {x}^{T}\widetilde{F}x + 2{\widetilde{g}}^{T}x + \widetilde{h} \leq 0}\right\} ,\] with \( \widetilde{F} \in {\mathbf{S}}_{+ + },\widetilde{h} - {\widetilde{g}}^{T}{\widetilde{F}}^{-1}\widetilde{g} < 0 \) . By the S-procedure,we see that \( \mathcal{E} \subseteq \widetilde{\mathcal{E}} \) if and only if there is a \( \lambda > 0 \) such that \[\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} \widetilde{F} & \widetilde{g} \\ {\widetilde{g}}^{T} & \widetilde{h} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \preccurlyeq \lambda \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} F & g \\ {g}^{T} & h \end{matrix}\right\rbrack .\] ---

pages.md: ### B.3 The field of values of two symmetric matrices The following result is the basis for the proof of the strong duality result in \( § \) B.1 and the S-procedure in \( § \) B.2. If \( A,B \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) ,then for all \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n} \) ,there exists an \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) such that \[{x}^{T}{Ax} = \mathbf{{tr}}\left( {AX}\right) ,\;{x}^{T}{Bx} = \mathbf{{tr}}\left( {BX}\right) . \tag{B.8}\] Remark B.1 Geometric interpretation. This result has an interesting interpretation in terms of the set --- \[W\left( {A,B}\right) = \left\{ {\left( {{x}^{T}{Ax},{x}^{T}{Bx}}\right) \mid x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n}}\right\} ,\] which is a cone in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) . It is the cone generated by the set \[F\left( {A,B}\right) = \left\{ {\left( {{x}^{T}{Ax},{x}^{T}{Bx}}\right) \mid \parallel x{\parallel }_{2} = 1}\right\} ,\] which is called the 2-dimensional field of values of the pair \( \left( {A,B}\right) \) . Geometrically, \( W\left( {A,B}\right) \) is the image of the set of rank-one positive semidefinite matrices under the linear transformation \( f : {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) defined by \[f\left( X\right) = \left( {\operatorname{tr}\left( {AX}\right) ,\operatorname{tr}\left( {BX}\right) }\right) .\] The result that for every \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n} \) there exists an \( x \) satisfying (B.8) means that \[W\left( {A,B}\right) = f\left( {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n}\right) .\] In other words, \( W\left( {A,B}\right) \) is a convex cone. --- The proof is constructive and uses induction on the rank of \( X \) . Suppose it is true for all \( X \in {\mathbf{S}}_{ + }^{n} \) with \( 1 \leq \operatorname{rank}X \leq k \) ,where \( k \geq 2 \) ,that there exists an \( x \) such that (B.8) holds. pages.md: ## Bibliography The results in this appendix are known under different names in different disciplines. The term S-procedure is from control; see Boyd, El Ghaoui, Feron, and Balakrishnan [BEFB94, pages 23, 33] for a survey and references. Variations of the S-procedure are known in linear algebra in the context of joint diagonalization of a pair of symmetric matrices; see, for example, Calabi [Cal64] and Uhlig [Uhl79]. Special cases of the strong duality result are studied in the nonlinear programming literature on trust-region methods (Stern and Wolkowicz [SW95], Nocedal and Wright [NW99, page 78]). Brickman [Bri61] proves that the field of values of a pair of matrices \( A,B \in {\mathbf{S}}^{n} \) (i.e.,the set \( F\left( {A,B}\right) \) defined in remark B.1) is a convex set if \( n > 2 \) ,and that the set \( W\left( {A,B}\right) \) is a convex cone (for any \( n \) ). Our proof in \( § \) B. 3 is based on Hestenes [Hes68]. Many related results and additional references can be found in Horn and Johnson [HJ91, §1.8] and Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [BTN01, §4.10.5].

## Appendix C Numerical linear algebra background

In this appendix we give a brief overview of some basic numerical linear algebra, concentrating on methods for solving one or more sets of linear equations. We focus on direct (i.e., noniterative) methods, and how problem structure can be exploited to improve efficiency. There are many important issues and methods in numerical linear algebra that we do not consider here, including numerical stability, details of matrix factorizations, methods for parallel or multiple processors, and iterative methods. For these (and other) topics, we refer the reader to the references given at the end of this appendix.

### C.1 Matrix structure and algorithm complexity

We concentrate on methods for solving the set of linear equations

\[{Ax} = b \tag{C.1}\]

where \( A \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times  n} \) and \( b \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . We assume \( A \) is nonsingular,so the solution is unique for all values of \( b \) ,and given by \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) . This basic problem arises in many optimization algorithms, and often accounts for most of the computation. In the context of solving the linear equations (C.1),the matrix \( A \) is often called the coefficient matrix,and the vector \( b \) is called the righthand side.

The standard generic methods for solving (C.1) require a computational effort that grows approximately like \( {n}^{3} \) . These methods assume nothing more about \( A \) than nonsingularity,and so are generally applicable. For \( n \) several hundred or smaller, these generic methods are probably the best methods to use, except in the most demanding real-time applications. For \( n \) more than a thousand or so,the generic methods of solving \( {Ax} = b \) become less practical.

pages.md: ## Coefficient matrix structure In many cases the coefficient matrix \( A \) has some special structure or form that can be exploited to solve the equation \( {Ax} = b \) more efficiently,using methods tailored for the special structure. For example,in the Newton system \( {\nabla }^{2}f\left( x\right) \Delta {x}_{\text{ nt }} = \; - \nabla f\left( x\right) \) ,the coefficient matrix is symmetric and positive definite,which allows us to use a solution method that is around twice as fast as the generic method (and also has better roundoff properties). There are many other types of structure that can be exploited, with computational savings (or algorithm speedup) that is usually far more than a factor of two. In many cases, the effort is reduced to something proportional to \( {n}^{2} \) or even \( n \) ,as compared to \( {n}^{3} \) for the generic methods. Since these methods are usually applied when \( n \) is at least a hundred,and often far larger, the savings can be dramatic. A wide variety of coefficient matrix structures can be exploited. Simple examples related to the sparsity pattern (i.e., the pattern of zero and nonzero entries in the matrix) include banded, block diagonal, or sparse matrices. A more subtle exploitable structure is diagonal plus low rank. Many common forms of convex optimization problems lead to linear equations with coefficient matrices that have these exploitable structures. (There are many other matrix structures that can be exploited, e.g., Toeplitz, Hankel, and circulant, that we will not consider in this appendix.) We refer to a generic method that does not exploit any sparsity pattern in the matrices as one for dense matrices. We refer to a method that does not exploit any structure at all in the matrices as one for unstructured matrices. #### C.1.1 Complexity analysis via flop count The cost of a numerical linear algebra algorithm is often expressed by giving the total number of floating-point operations or flops required to carry it out, as a function of various problem dimensions. We define a flop as one addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division of two floating-point numbers. (Some authors define a flop as one multiplication followed by one addition, so their flop counts are smaller by a factor up to two.) To evaluate the complexity of an algorithm, we count the total number of flops, express it as a function (usually a polynomial) of the dimensions of the matrices and vectors involved, and simplify the expression by ignoring all terms except the leading (i.e., highest order or dominant) terms. As an example, suppose that a particular algorithm requires a total of \[{m}^{3} + 3{m}^{2}n + {mn} + {4m}{n}^{2} + {5m} + {22}\] flops,where \( m \) and \( n \) are problem dimensions. We would normally simplify this flop count to \[{m}^{3} + 3{m}^{2}n + {4m}{n}^{2}\] flops,since these are the leading terms in the problem dimensions \( m \) and \( n \) . If in addition we assumed that \( m \ll n \) ,we would further simplify the flop count to \( {4m}{n}^{2} \) .

A more subtle exploitable structure is diagonal plus low rank. Many common forms of convex optimization problems lead to linear equations with coefficient matrices that have these exploitable structures. (There are many other matrix structures that can be exploited, e.g., Toeplitz, Hankel, and circulant, that we will not consider in this appendix.)

We refer to a generic method that does not exploit any sparsity pattern in the matrices as one for dense matrices. We refer to a method that does not exploit any structure at all in the matrices as one for unstructured matrices.
C.1.1 Complexity analysis via flop count

The cost of a numerical linear algebra algorithm is often expressed by giving the total number of floating-point operations or flops required to carry it out, as a function of various problem dimensions. We define a flop as one addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division of two floating-point numbers. (Some authors define a flop as one multiplication followed by one addition, so their flop counts are smaller by a factor up to two.) To evaluate the complexity of an algorithm, we count the total number of flops, express it as a function (usually a polynomial) of the dimensions of the matrices and vectors involved, and simplify the expression by ignoring all terms except the leading (i.e., highest order or dominant) terms.

pages.md: Flop counts were originally popularized when floating-point operations were relatively slow, so counting the number gave a good estimate of the total computation time. This is no longer the case: Issues such as cache boundaries and locality of reference can dramatically affect the computation time of a numerical algorithm. However, flop counts can still give us a good rough estimate of the computation time of a numerical algorithm, and how the time grows with increasing problem size. Since a flop count no longer accurately predicts the computation time of an algorithm, we usually pay most attention to its order or orders, i.e., its largest exponents, and ignore differences in flop counts smaller than a factor of two or so. For example,an algorithm with flop count \( 5{n}^{2} \) is considered comparable to one with a flop count \( 4{n}^{2} \) ,but faster than an algorithm with flop count \( \left( {1/3}\right) {n}^{3} \) . #### C.1.2 Cost of basic matrix-vector operations ## Vector operations To compute the inner product \( {x}^{T}y \) of two vectors \( x,y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) we form the products \( {x}_{i}{y}_{i} \) ,and then add them,which requires \( n \) multiplies and \( n - 1 \) additions,or \( {2n} - 1 \) flops. As mentioned above, we keep only the leading term, and say that the inner product requires \( {2n} \) flops,or even more approximately,order \( n \) flops. A scalar-vector multiplication \( {\alpha x} \) ,where \( \alpha \in \mathbf{R} \) and \( x \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) costs \( n \) flops. The addition \( x + y \) of two vectors \( x,y \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) also costs \( n \) flops. If the vectors \( x \) and \( y \) are sparse,i.e.,have only a few nonzero terms,these basic operations can be carried out faster (assuming the vectors are stored using an appropriate data structure). For example,if \( x \) is a sparse vector with \( N \) nonzero entries,then the inner product \( {x}^{T}y \) can be computed in \( {2N} \) flops. ## Matrix-vector multiplication A matrix-vector multiplication \( y = {Ax} \) where \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) costs \( {2mn} \) flops: We have to calculate \( m \) components of \( y \) ,each of which is the product of a row of \( A \) with \( x \) ,i.e.,an inner product of two vectors in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Matrix-vector products can often be accelerated by taking advantage of structure in \( A \) . For example,if \( A \) is diagonal,then \( {Ax} \) can be computed in \( n \) flops, instead of \( 2{n}^{2} \) flops for multiplication by a general \( n \times n \) matrix. More generally,if \( A \) is sparse,with only \( N \) nonzero elements (out of \( {mn} \) ),then \( {2N} \) flops are needed to form \( {Ax} \) ,since we can skip multiplications and additions with zero. As a less obvious example,suppose the matrix \( A \) has rank \( p \ll \min \{ m,n\} \) ,and is represented (stored) in the factored form \( A = {UV} \) ,where \( U \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times p},V \in {\mathbf{R}}^{p \times n} \) . Then we can compute \( {Ax} \) by first computing \( {Vx} \) (which costs \( {2pn} \) flops),and then computing \( U\left( {Vx}\right) \) (which costs \( {2mp} \) flops),so the total is \( {2p}\left( {m + n}\right) \) flops. Since \( p \ll \min \{ m,n\} \) ,this is small compared to \( {2mn} \) . ## Matrix-matrix multiplication The matrix-matrix product \( C = {AB} \) ,where \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{m \times n} \) and \( B \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times p} \) ,costs \( {2mnp} \) flops. We have \( {mp} \) elements in \( C \) to calculate,each of which is an inner product of two vectors of length \( n \) . Again,we can often make substantial savings by taking advantage of structure in \( A \) and \( B \) . For example,if \( A \) and \( B \) are sparse,we can accelerate the multiplication by skipping additions and multiplications with zero. If \( m = p \) and we know that \( C \) is symmetric,then we can calculate the matrix product in \( {m}^{2}n \) flops,since we only have to compute the \( \left( {1/2}\right) m\left( {m + 1}\right) \) elements in the lower triangular part.

C.2.1 Linear equations that are easy to solve
We start by examining some cases for which \( {Ax} = b \) is easily solved,i.e., \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) is easily computed.

Suppose \( A \) is diagonal and nonsingular (i.e., \( {a}_{ii} \neq  0 \) for all \( i \) ). The set of linear equations \( {Ax} = b \) can be written as \( {a}_{ii}{x}_{i} = {b}_{i},i = 1,\ldots ,n \) . The solution is given by \( {x}_{i} = {b}_{i}/{a}_{ii} \) ,and can be calculated in \( n \) flops.

A matrix \( A \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times  n} \) is lower triangular if \( {a}_{ij} = 0 \) for \( j > i \) . pages.md: Suppose \( A \) is lower triangular and nonsingular. The equations \( {Ax} = b \) are \[\left\lbrack \begin{matrix} {a}_{11} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {a}_{n1} & {a}_{n2} & \cdots & {a}_{nn} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} {x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ \vdots \\ {x}_{n} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{matrix} {b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2} \\ \vdots \\ {b}_{n} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack\] From the first row,we have \( {a}_{11}{x}_{1} = {b}_{1} \) ,from which we conclude \( {x}_{1} = {b}_{1}/{a}_{11} \) . From the second row we have \( {a}_{21}{x}_{1} + {a}_{22}{x}_{2} = {b}_{2} \) ,so we can express \( {x}_{2} \) as \( {x}_{2} = \; \left( {{b}_{2} - {a}_{21}{x}_{1}}\right) /{a}_{22} \) . (We have already computed \( {x}_{1} \) ,so every number on the righthand side is known.) Continuing this way,we can express each component of \( x \) in terms of previous components, yielding the algorithm \[{x}_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {b}_{1}/{a}_{11}\] \[{x}_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{2} - {a}_{21}{x}_{1}}\right) /{a}_{22}\] \[{x}_{3} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{3} - {a}_{31}{x}_{1} - {a}_{32}{x}_{2}}\right) /{a}_{33}\] \[\vdots\] \[{x}_{n} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{n} - {a}_{n1}{x}_{1} - {a}_{n2}{x}_{2} - \cdots - {a}_{n,n - 1}{x}_{n - 1}}\right) /{a}_{nn}.\] This procedure is called forward substitution, since we successively compute the components of \( x \) by substituting the known values into the next equation. Let us give a flop count for forward substitution. We start by calculating \( {x}_{1}(1 \) flop). We substitute \( {x}_{1} \) in the second equation to find \( {x}_{2} \) (3 flops),then substitute \( {x}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{2} \) in the third equation to find \( {x}_{3} \) (5 flops),etc. The total number of flops is \[1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + \left( {{2n} - 1}\right) = {n}^{2}.\] Thus,when \( A \) is lower triangular and nonsingular,we can compute \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) in \( {n}^{2} \) flops. If the matrix \( A \) has additional structure,in addition to being lower triangular, then forward substitution can be more efficient than \( {n}^{2} \) flops. For example,if \( A \) is sparse (or banded),with at most \( k \) nonzero entries per row,then each forward substitution step requires at most \( {2k} + 1 \) flops,so the overall flop count is \( 2\left( {k + 1}\right) n \) , or \( {2kn} \) after dropping the term \( {2n} \) . ## Upper triangular matrices A matrix \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is upper triangular if \( {A}^{T} \) is lower triangular,i.e.,if \( {a}_{ij} = 0 \) for \( j < i \) . We can solve linear equations with nonsingular upper triangular coefficient matrix in a way similar to forward substitution, except that we start by calculating \( {x}_{n} \) ,then \( {x}_{n - 1} \) ,and so on. The algorithm is \[{x}_{n} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {b}_{n}/{a}_{nn}\] \[{x}_{n - 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{n - 1} - {a}_{n - 1,n}{x}_{n}}\right) /{a}_{n - 1,n - 1}\] \[{x}_{n - 2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{n - 2} - {a}_{n - 2,n - 1}{x}_{n - 1} - {a}_{n - 2,n}{x}_{n}}\right) /{a}_{n - 2,n - 2}\] \[\vdots\] \[{x}_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{b}_{1} - {a}_{12}{x}_{2} - {a}_{13}{x}_{3} - \cdots - {a}_{1n}{x}_{n}}\right) /{a}_{11}.\]

In this case we can compute \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) by a simple matrix-vector product \( x = {A}^{T}b \) ,which costs \( 2{n}^{2} \) in general. If the matrix \( A \) has additional structure,we can compute \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) even more efficiently than \( 2{n}^{2} \) flops. For example,if \( A \) has the form \( A = I - {2u}{u}^{T} \) ,where \( \parallel u{\parallel }_{2} = 1 \) ,we can compute \[x = {A}^{-1}b = {\left( I - 2u{u}^{T}\right) }^{T}b = b - 2\left( {{u}^{T}b}\right) u\] by first computing \( {u}^{T}b \) ,then forming \( b - 2\left( {{u}^{T}b}\right) u \) ,which costs \( {4n} \) flops. ## Permutation matrices Let \( \pi = \left( {{\pi }_{1},\ldots ,{\pi }_{n}}\right) \) be a permutation of \( \left( {1,2,\ldots ,n}\right) \) . This turns out to be \( {A}^{T} \) ,which shows that permutation matrices are orthogonal. If \( A \) is a permutation matrix,solving \( {Ax} = b \) is very easy: \( x \) is obtained by permuting the entries of \( b \) by \( {\pi }^{-1} \) . This requires no floating point operations, according to our definition (but, depending on the implementation, might involve copying floating point numbers). We can reach the same conclusion from the equation \( x = {A}^{T}b \) . The matrix \( {A}^{T} \) (like \( A \) ) has only one nonzero entry per row,with value one. The step of expressing \( A \) in factored form (i.e.,computing the factors \( {A}_{i} \) ) is called the factorization step,and the process of computing \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) recursively, by solving a sequence problems of the form \( {A}_{i}{z}_{i} = {z}_{i - 1} \) ,is often called the solve step. The total flop count for solving \( {Ax} = b \) using this factor-solve method is \( f + s \) , where \( f \) is the flop count for computing the factorization,and \( s \) is the total flop count for the solve step. In many cases, the cost of the factorization, f, dominates the total solve cost \( s \) . In this case,the cost of solving \( {Ax} = b \) ,i.e.,computing \( x = {A}^{-1}b \) ,is just \( f \) . ## Solving equations with multiple righthand sides Suppose we need to solve the equations \[A{x}_{1} = {b}_{1},\;A{x}_{2} = {b}_{2},\;\ldots ,\;A{x}_{m} = {b}_{m},\] where \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is nonsingular. In other words,we need to solve \( m \) sets of linear equations, with the same coefficient matrix, but different righthand sides. Alternatively, we can think of this as computing the matrix \[X = {A}^{-1}B\] where \[X = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{llll} {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & \cdots & {x}_{m} \end{array}\right\rbrack \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times m},\;B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{llll} {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & \cdots & {b}_{m} \end{array}\right\rbrack \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times m}.\] To do this,we first factor \( A \) ,which costs \( f \) . Then for \( i = 1,\ldots ,m \) we compute \( {A}^{-1}{b}_{i} \) using the solve step. Since we only factor \( A \) once,the total effort is \[f + {ms}\text{ . }\] In other words,we amortize the factorization cost over the set of \( m \) solves. Had we (needlessly) repeated the factorization step for each \( i \) ,the cost would be \( m\left( {f + s}\right) \) . When the factorization cost \( f \) dominates the solve cost \( s \) ,the factor-solve method allows us to solve a small number of linear systems, with the same coefficient matrix, at essentially the same cost as solving one. This is because the most expensive step, the factorization, is done only once.

pages.md: We can use the factor-solve method to compute the inverse \( {A}^{-1} \) by solving \( {Ax} = {e}_{i} \) for \( i = 1,\ldots ,n \) ,i.e.,by computing \( {A}^{-1}I \) . This requires one factorization and \( n \) solves,so the cost is \( f + {ns} \) . ### C.3 LU, Cholesky, and LDL \( {}^{T} \) factorization #### C.3.1 LU factorization Every nonsingular matrix \( A \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) can be factored as \[A = {PLU}\] where \( P \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is a permutation matrix, \( L \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is unit lower triangular,and \( U \in {\mathbf{R}}^{n \times n} \) is upper triangular and nonsingular. This is called the LU factorization of \( A \) . We can also write the factorization as \( {P}^{T}A = {LU} \) ,where the matrix \( {P}^{T}A \) is obtained from \( A \) by re-ordering the rows. The standard algorithm for computing an LU factorization is called Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting or Gaussian elimination with row pivoting. The cost is \( \left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3} \) flops if no structure in \( A \) is exploited, which is the case we consider first. ## Solving sets of linear equations using the LU factorization The LU factorization, combined with the factor-solve approach, is the standard method for solving a general set of linear equations \( {Ax} = b \) . Algorithm C. 1 Solving linear equations by LU factorization. --- given a set of linear equations \( {Ax} = b \) ,with \( A \) nonsingular. 1. LU factorization. Factor \( A \) as \( A = {PLU}\left( {\left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3}\text{ flops }}\right) \) . 2. Permutation. Solve \( P{z}_{1} = b \) (0 flops). 3. Forward substitution. Solve \( L{z}_{2} = {z}_{1}\left( {n}^{2}\right. \) flops \( ) \) . 4. Backward substitution. Solve \( {Ux} = {z}_{2}\left( {n}^{2}\right. \) flops \( ) \) . --- The total cost is \( \left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3} + 2{n}^{2} \) ,or \( \left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3} \) flops if we keep only the leading term. If we need to solve multiple sets of linear equations with different righthand sides,i.e., \( A{x}_{i} = {b}_{i},i = 1,\ldots ,m \) ,the cost is \[\left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3} + {2m}{n}^{2},\] since we factor \( A \) once,and carry out \( m \) pairs of forward and backward substitutions. For example, we can solve two sets of linear equations, with the same coefficient matrix but different righthand sides, at essentially the same cost as solving one. We can compute the inverse \( {A}^{-1} \) by solving the equations \( A{x}_{i} = {e}_{i} \) , where \( {x}_{i} \) is the \( i \) th column of \( {A}^{-1} \) ,and \( {e}_{i} \) is the \( i \) th unit vector. This costs \( \left( {8/3}\right) {n}^{3} \) , i.e.,about \( 3{n}^{3} \) flops. If the matrix \( A \) has certain structure,for example banded or sparse,the LU factorization can be computed in less than \( \left( {2/3}\right) {n}^{3} \) flops,and the associated forward and backward substitutions can also be carried out more efficiently.
